accountants.title: CPA & Accountant Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
accountants.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for CPAs and accountants. Protect your income against cognitive impairment, burnout from tax-season intensity, and mental health conditions. See how carriers differ on mental/nervous limitation clauses.
accountants.tldr: Accountants commonly qualify for a 6A occupation class, one of the most favorable tiers, making disability insurance cost-effective relative to income protected. Own-occupation coverage is critical because accounting demands sustained cognitive precision that neurological or psychological conditions can impair, even when physical capacity remains intact. The contract language governing cognitive disability and mental health provisions deserves the most scrutiny, because those pathways represent your highest disability risk.

anesthesiologists.title: Disability Insurance for Anesthesiologists | Own-Occupation Coverage
anesthesiologists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for anesthesiologists. Protect your income against spinal disc disease from prolonged standing, needlestick exposure, and fine motor loss affecting intubation and regional techniques.
anesthesiologists.tldr: Anesthesiologists face high disability risk centered on spinal health and fine motor control despite favorable occupational class ratings. Own-occupation coverage is non-negotiable because back and neck injuries can prevent you from standing through cases even when you retain the ability to work in other medical roles, and the policy must protect your anesthesia-specific income. Specialized guidance addresses occupational hazards (needlestick exposure, substance sensitization) and makes sure your contract doesn't define you generically as a 'physician' where insurers could argue lower-paying medical work is available.

architects.title: Architect Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
architects.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for licensed architects. Protect your income against progressive vision loss, neurological conditions impairing spatial reasoning, and chronic pain from sustained design work.
architects.tldr: Most licensed architects qualify for favorable 5A or 6A occupation class ratings, keeping disability insurance premiums competitive relative to income protected. Own-occupation coverage is critical because architecture requires cognitive, visual, and creative capacity beyond general office work; visual impairment or neurological conditions can eliminate your ability to practice even if other work remains possible. The contract language and carrier match should fit your practice structure, whether you're a principal, independent practitioner, or firm employee.

attorneys.title: Attorney Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
attorneys.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for attorneys. A claim is decided by the definition type applied to your real duties, and most attorneys can secure full-period mental health coverage.
attorneys.tldr: For an attorney, the provisions that decide a claim are the own-occupation definition type and your residual coverage, not whether the contract names litigation or transactional work. A claim is measured against the material duties you were actually performing when disability began. Most attorneys are not in the high-risk group that faces a forced 24-month mental and nervous cap, so full-benefit-period mental health coverage is generally available across the carriers we place. Terms lock at underwriting, where roughly 28 percent of the policies in our 2026 audit carried an exclusion or rating, so applying while healthy is the real lever.

business-finance.title: Business & Finance Disability Insurance
business-finance.description: Seaworthy Insurance places disability insurance for executives, business owners, attorneys, accountants, and financial professionals. All five major carriers compared on own-occupation language, occupation class, and how each handles variable and equity compensation.
business-finance.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places coverage for executives, business owners, attorneys, accountants, and financial professionals across all five major carriers, evaluating own-occupation language, occupation class, how each carrier counts variable and equity pay, and premium.

business-owners.title: Disability Insurance for Business Owners | Own-Occupation Coverage
business-owners.description: Business owners face two exposures: personal income that stops and business costs that do not. Compare individual coverage plus Business Overhead Expense, where Ameritas writes the highest limit.
business-owners.tldr: A business owner has two distinct exposures when disability hits: personal income that stops, and business operating costs that do not. Individual disability insurance protects the first; Business Overhead Expense, buy-sell, and key-person coverage protect the second. The right structure depends on how you take income, whether you have partners, and what the business owes. Of the carriers we place, Ameritas writes the highest BOE limit, $100,000 of monthly expense reimbursement versus roughly $50,000 at the others.

crna-quote-comparison.title: CRNA Disability Insurance: Carrier Comparison
crna-quote-comparison.description: How the five major disability carriers, Guardian, MassMutual, Principal, Ameritas, and The Standard, classify, underwrite, and cover CRNAs. Occupation class, own-occupation definitions, riders, and exclusions vary in ways that affect both premium and whether a claim pays.
crna-quote-comparison.tldr: Across the five major disability carriers, CRNA occupation class, own-occupation definitions, and rider structure vary enough that the same CRNA profile produces materially different policies and premiums. The right carrier generally depends on practice setting, health history, and which contract provisions matter most for anesthesia work. In Seaworthy's CRNA placements, MassMutual and Principal are selected most often, with the comparison run across all five carriers before any recommendation.

crnas.title: CRNA Disability Insurance
crnas.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in disability insurance for CRNAs and nurse anesthetists. All five top carriers compared, with each carrier's own-occupation definition reviewed for anesthesia providers.
crnas.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places CRNA coverage across all five major carriers, with every quote evaluated against occupation class, own-occupation contract language, rider structure, and premium.

data-scientists.title: Disability Insurance for Data Scientists & ML Engineers | Own-Occupation
data-scientists.description: Disability insurance for data scientists, data engineers, and ML engineers in the AI boom. Coverage that protects advanced quantitative and modeling work through a true own-occupation definition, sized to fast-rising AI-era compensation, with the top 6A occupation class and all five carriers compared.
data-scientists.tldr: Data scientists, data engineers, and ML engineers are at the center of the AI hiring surge, where pay is high and climbing fast. The field is newer, so many of these high earners are making a coverage decision for the first time, and two things deserve the most attention: a true own-occupation definition that protects advanced quantitative reasoning and statistical or machine-learning modeling rather than letting a carrier collapse it into generic computer work, and a benefit sized to AI-era total compensation. These roles also sit in the top 6A occupation class, which means strong contract terms and competitive pricing. We run all five major carriers on every case.

dental-hygienists.title: Disability Insurance for Dental Hygienists | Own-Occupation Coverage
dental-hygienists.description: Disability insurance for dental hygienists, including how carriers classify hygienists, why the market is narrower than it is for dentists, the modified own-occupation contract available to age 65, and the $8,000 monthly benefit ceiling.
dental-hygienists.tldr: Dental hygienists can secure individual disability coverage, and the terms differ from a dentist's in ways worth understanding before shopping. The practical placement is a modified own-occupation contract to age 65 with a monthly benefit capped at $8,000 and a 24-month mental health benefit.

dentist-anesthesiologists.title: Dentist Anesthesiologist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
dentist-anesthesiologists.description: Compare disability insurance for dentist anesthesiologists. An ADA-recognized dental specialty underwritten as a dentist, classed 3D at The Standard, with specialty deeming and the anesthesia-group mental and nervous limitation to plan around.
dentist-anesthesiologists.tldr: Dentist anesthesiologists are an ADA-recognized dental specialty and are underwritten as dentists, classed 3D at The Standard, which qualifies for its Own Occupation Rider, with specialty deeming available so a claim is measured against dental anesthesia rather than dentistry broadly. The one provision that differs from a general dentist's is the mental and nervous limitation. Because the work combines dentistry and anesthesia, both of which sit in the carriers' high-risk mental and nervous group, the 24-month limitation is typically required rather than optional. The priorities at application are a true own-occupation definition for the sedation and airway work, a residual rider, and applying before any health history accumulates.

dentists.title: Dentist Disability Insurance
dentists.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in dentist disability insurance. All five major carriers compared, with each carrier's own-occupation definition reviewed for clinical dental work and dental specialties.
dentists.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places dentist coverage across all five major carriers, with every quote evaluated against occupation class, own-occupation contract language including ADA-specialty deeming, rider structure, and premium.

emergency-medicine.title: Emergency Medicine Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
emergency-medicine.description: Disability insurance for emergency physicians: EM sits in the higher-risk class tier at every major carrier, the 24-month mental health limitation is mandatory, and Principal caps EM issue amounts at $20,000 a month. How to structure coverage around those constraints.
emergency-medicine.tldr: Every major carrier places emergency medicine in its higher-risk physician tier, per the mid-2026 producer guides, and the specialty is on the nearly identical mandatory lists that cap mental and nervous claims at 24 months, so the full-period election available to most physicians is generally off the table for EM. Principal also caps its EM tier at a $20,000 monthly issue limit where its higher physician classes reach $30,000. Structure and timing carry the weight here: a true own-occupation definition, a residual rider, and an application filed before shift work leaves a medical history.

endodontists.title: Endodontist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
endodontists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for endodontists. Protect against cervical disc disease from microscope positioning, carpal tunnel from file manipulation, and visual strain. See how carriers cover gradual loss of microsurgical precision.
endodontists.tldr: Endodontists are underwritten as dentists, classed 3D at The Standard, which qualifies for its Own Occupation Rider, with disability risk concentrated in hand function, cervical spine health, and visual acuity, where microsurgical precision within fractions of a millimeter is non-negotiable. Musculoskeletal conditions (cervical disc disease, carpal tunnel, de Quervain tendinopathy) are the leading disability pathways. The own-occupation definition must specifically protect endodontic practice, not reduce you to general-dentistry income, and a residual rider is critical given the likelihood of gradual decline rather than sudden total disability.

engineers.title: Engineer Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
engineers.description: Compare disability insurance quotes for engineers. Protect your income against cognitive impairment, TBI, and neurological conditions that threaten mathematical reasoning and systems analysis. See how carriers rate field vs. office engineering roles.
engineers.tldr: Engineers typically qualify for 5A or 6A occupational class ratings in office-based roles, with lower classifications for field-based specialties. Disability risk is centered on cognitive function; neurological conditions, traumatic brain injury, stroke, or cognitive effects of medical treatment can end engineering careers by impairing mathematical reasoning and systems-thinking capacity. Own-occupation coverage is essential because 'any occupation' definitions allow carriers to deny claims based on generic computer work, ignoring the difference between data entry and professional engineering analysis.

family-medicine.title: Family Medicine Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
family-medicine.description: Disability insurance for family physicians: near-best occupation classes at every major carrier, full-period mental health elections, part-time and locum underwriting paths, and business overhead expense coverage for practice owners.
family-medicine.tldr: Family medicine is one of the least expensive physician specialties to insure. The specialty sits in each major carrier's best or near-best physician class, and family physicians can elect full-benefit-period mental health coverage. The real coverage questions are structural: sizing benefits against a leaner income ceiling, insuring part-time and locum arrangements at carriers that accept them, and adding business overhead expense coverage when the physician owns the practice.

general-dentists.title: General Dentist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
general-dentists.description: Own-occupation disability insurance for general dentists: how carriers class general practice, why the 24-month mental and nervous limitation applies to general dentistry across the major carriers, what production-paid associates and practice owners each need, and when to apply.
general-dentists.tldr: General dentists are the largest group of dentists Seaworthy covers, and their protection turns on the same contract details a specialist's does. A true own-occupation definition keeps benefits paying when a disability ends clinical dentistry, even if teaching, consulting, or practice administration remains possible. Carriers commonly class general dentists at 3D, and MassMutual upgrades a dentist from 3D to 4D after an AEGD or GPR residency. One provision deserves extra attention: general dentistry sits in the high-risk mental and nervous group at several major carriers, where the 24-month limitation is required rather than optional. Associates paid on production should size the benefit to total documented earnings, and practice owners usually pair personal coverage with business overhead expense.

geriatricians.title: Geriatrician Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
geriatricians.description: Compare disability insurance quotes for geriatricians. Protect against compassion fatigue, infectious disease exposure in long-term care settings, and musculoskeletal strain from patient handling. See which carriers offer extended mental health benefits.
geriatricians.tldr: Geriatricians manage the most medically complex patients in medicine while bearing the psychological weight of end-of-life care and compassion fatigue. A 24-month cap on mental and nervous claims would be a poor fit for a specialty where burnout is endemic rather than exceptional, and geriatricians do not have to accept one: the specialty is not in the high-risk group forced into the cap, so full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage is available across the major carriers. Disability risk spans cognitive (multi-system disease management), physical (patient handling), and psychological (moral distress) domains; own-occupation coverage with the full-period mental health election is the structure that fits.

infectious-disease.title: Infectious Disease Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
infectious-disease.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for infectious disease physicians. Protect your income against bloodborne pathogen exposure, needle stick injuries, and burnout from managing critically ill patients. See how carriers handle occupational infection risk.
infectious-disease.tldr: Infectious disease specialists qualify for favorable occupational classifications, but own-occupation coverage is essential because your income depends entirely on cognitive diagnostic capacity. Pathogen exposure, burnout from managing critically ill patients, and occupational psychological stress are the specialty's real disability pathways, and ID is not in the high-risk group forced into the 24-month mental and nervous cap, so full-benefit-period coverage is available and worth electing.

internal-medicine.title: Internal Medicine Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
internal-medicine.description: Disability insurance for internists: a top-tier occupation class at every major carrier, full-benefit-period mental health elections, and the pre-fellowship timing play that locks internal-medicine pricing for a subspecialty career.
internal-medicine.tldr: Internal medicine occupies a favorable corner of the disability market: the specialty sits in each major carrier's best or near-best physician class, which makes coverage relatively inexpensive per dollar of benefit, and internists are not in the high-risk group forced into a 24-month mental health cap, so full-benefit-period coverage is available. The class advantage is also a timing argument, since an internist headed toward a procedural fellowship can lock internal-medicine pricing on a policy issued before the subspecialty declares itself. Internal medicine is among the most common physician specialties in Seaworthy's placed book.

nephrologists.title: Nephrologist Disability Insurance: Compare Top Carriers
nephrologists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for nephrologists. Coverage built for burnout, dialysis exposure, and procedural risk.
nephrologists.tldr: Nephrologists need own-occupation coverage that protects against burnout and psychiatric disability from managing chronically ill patients with high mortality rates. Mental health provisions are critical, and nephrology is not in the high-risk group forced into the 24-month mental and nervous cap, so full-benefit-period coverage is available across the major carriers and worth electing in a specialty where burnout is a documented occupational pathway. Infectious disease exposure in dialysis environments adds procedural disability risk.

obgyn.title: Disability Insurance for OB/GYN | Own-Occupation Coverage
obgyn.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for OB/GYNs. Protect your income against back injury from delivery positioning, burnout from unpredictable call, and malpractice-related psychological disability. See how carriers treat obstetric vs. gynecologic practice mix.
obgyn.tldr: OB/GYNs require own-occupation coverage that protects the full hybrid practice, obstetric care and operative gynecology together. Unpredictable on-call scheduling drives cumulative burnout and sleep deprivation, and OB/GYN is not in the high-risk group forced into the 24-month mental and nervous cap, so full-benefit-period mental health coverage is available and worth electing. Back injuries from delivery positioning and cesarean work are the most common physical trigger; an individual policy bought while the record is clean covers occupational back and neck injury for the full benefit period.

ophthalmologists.title: Ophthalmologist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
ophthalmologists.description: Disability insurance for ophthalmologists. Carriers disagree on how to class this microsurgical specialty more than almost any other, from 3P at MassMutual to 5M at Principal and Ameritas, and an ophthalmologist's income depends on their own vision and fine motor control. Guardian's surgical-income enhancement and a true own-occupation definition are the decisions that matter.
ophthalmologists.tldr: Ophthalmology is a microsurgical specialty whose income rests on two things the surgeon cannot replace, their own eyesight and their fine motor control, so a tremor or a decline in vision is career-ending even when the ophthalmologist stays healthy otherwise. It is also among the specialties carriers class most inconsistently, running from 3P at MassMutual, which groups it with surgeons, to 5M at Principal and Ameritas and 4S at The Standard, which means the same ophthalmologist can be priced across a wide range. The decisions that protect the income are Guardian's surgical-income enhancement, which deems an ophthalmologist disabled if they can no longer operate, and a true own-occupation definition that measures the claim against ophthalmology rather than medicine broadly.

optometrists.title: Disability Insurance for Optometrists | Own-Occupation Coverage
optometrists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for optometrists. Protect your income against vision loss, hand and wrist repetitive strain, and eye strain from prolonged slit lamp use. See how carriers cover the visual acuity demands unique to ODs.
optometrists.tldr: Optometrists need own-occupation coverage that explicitly covers vision loss and visual impairment as disability pathways, not as excluded conditions. Your ability to examine patients and interpret diagnostic findings depends entirely on your own visual function; policies must protect against the profession-specific risk that other healthcare professionals don't face.

oral-surgeons.title: Disability Insurance for Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons | Own-Occupation Coverage
oral-surgeons.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for oral and maxillofacial surgeons. Protect your surgical income against cervical spine strain, hand injury from forceful extractions, and needle stick exposure. See how carriers classify OMS versus general dentistry.
oral-surgeons.tldr: Oral and maxillofacial surgeons require own-occupation coverage that reflects the surgical scope of their practice, not general dentistry, and protects the substantial income difference. Cervical strain from confined operative field positioning and hand injury from forceful surgical movements are predictable occupational consequences; policies must cover these without imposing arbitrary benefit limits.

orthodontists.title: Orthodontist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
orthodontists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for orthodontists. Protect your income against carpal tunnel from high-volume wire adjustments, cervical disc disease, and eye strain from magnification. Get residual coverage and business overhead expense for practice owners.
orthodontists.tldr: Orthodontists face significant cumulative musculoskeletal risk from high-volume repetitive practice despite favorable occupational classifications. Own-occupation coverage with a residual rider is essential because partial disability from carpal tunnel, cervical disc disease, or hand conditions reduces income through lower patient throughput rather than ending the profession outright. Most orthodontists own their practices, so business overhead expense coverage, which protects the practice's fixed costs, usually belongs alongside the personal policy.

orthopedic-surgeons.title: Orthopedic Surgeon Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
orthopedic-surgeons.description: Disability insurance for orthopedic surgeons, a specialty with one of the widest occupation-class spreads in medicine (about two tiers, Ameritas 5M to Guardian and Principal 3M) and the one surgical specialty Guardian excludes from its surgeon discount. A physically punishing practice where the surgeon's own body is the risk.
orthopedic-surgeons.tldr: Orthopedic surgery has one of the widest occupation-class spreads in medicine, roughly two full tiers from 5M at Ameritas down to 3M at Guardian and Principal, so the same surgeon can be priced dramatically differently across the five carriers, and it is the one surgical specialty Guardian carves out of its surgeon discount. The risk is physical, since orthopedics is punishing and the surgeon's own back, hands, and joints are what a career-ending injury usually strikes. The decisions that protect the income are a true own-occupation definition, Guardian's surgical-income enhancement for surgeons earning most of their income from operating, and a residual rider for the more common partial claim.

otolaryngologists.title: ENT & Otolaryngologist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
otolaryngologists.description: Own-occupation disability insurance for otolaryngologists (ENT). Carriers class ENT mid-tier, from 4M up to Ameritas at 5M, so comparing all five is how a surgical income gets protected.
otolaryngologists.tldr: Otolaryngology, or ENT, is a medical-surgical hybrid, part office practice and part head-and-neck microsurgery, and that mix lands it in the middle of the physician range, from 4M at most carriers up to Ameritas at 5M as the favorable outlier. The career-critical function is fine motor control, because ear and endoscopic surgery run at fine tolerances, so a hand tremor or a neurological condition can end operative practice while leaving office ENT open. The decisions that protect the income are a true own-occupation definition and, for the surgery-heavy practitioner, Guardian's surgical-income enhancement.

pediatric-dentists.title: Pediatric Dentist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
pediatric-dentists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for pediatric dentists. Protect your income against extreme ergonomic strain from small-patient positioning, carpal tunnel from confined operative fields, and physical injury from behavior management. See how carriers classify pediatric dental risk.
pediatric-dentists.tldr: Pediatric dentists face extreme ergonomic strain from working with small patients in compromised positions for extended periods, combined with physical demands of behavior management and sustained fine motor precision. Carpal tunnel, back injury, neck strain, and loss of hand dexterity are common occupational risks. Own-occupation coverage secures full benefits when musculoskeletal disability prevents the precision dentistry work your specialty income depends on.

pediatricians.title: Pediatrician Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
pediatricians.description: Disability insurance for pediatricians, Principal's only top-6M physician specialty and priced at or near the best tier at every major carrier, with full mental-health coverage and the infectious and physical exposure of pediatric practice.
pediatricians.tldr: Pediatrics is the class darling of the physician disability market. It is the only specialty in Principal's top 6M medical class and sits at or near the best tier at every major carrier, which makes coverage inexpensive per dollar of benefit, and The Standard's discount for select specialties includes it. That favorable pricing protects a leaner income, since pediatricians earn less than most specialties they refer to, so the leaner ceiling changes how the benefit is sized without changing the reason to carry it. The specialty's real risks are the infectious exposure and physical demands of examining children, and full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage is available rather than the 24-month cap.

periodontists.title: Periodontist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
periodontists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for periodontists. Protect your surgical income against carpal tunnel from implant placement, cervical disc disease from sustained positioning, and hand tremor affecting microsurgical precision. Get residual coverage for reduced caseloads.
periodontists.tldr: Periodontists perform high-precision surgical techniques requiring sustained hand dexterity, fine motor control, and extreme ergonomic positioning. Carpal tunnel, hand tremor, back and neck injury from prolonged positioning, and repetitive strain affecting surgical precision are career-ending injuries. Own-occupation coverage secures full benefits when hand loss or musculoskeletal disability prevents the surgical periodontal work your specialty income depends on.

pharmacists.title: Pharmacist Disability Insurance | PharmD Quote Comparison
pharmacists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for pharmacists. Protect your income against cognitive decline affecting drug interaction verification, lower back pain from prolonged standing, and repetitive strain from high-volume dispensing. See how carriers classify PharmD roles.
pharmacists.tldr: Pharmacists depend on cognitive function and specialized pharmaceutical knowledge that cannot be replaced in non-pharmacy roles. Cognitive decline, memory loss, psychiatric disability preventing decision-making, or burnout that compromises your ability to verify prescriptions safely is career-ending. Own-occupation coverage secures full benefits when cognitive or psychiatric disability prevents the clinical pharmacist work that generates your income.

physician-assistants.title: Physician Assistant Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
physician-assistants.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for physician assistants. Protect your procedural and clinical income against needle stick exposure, musculoskeletal injury, and burnout. See how carriers classify PAs by specialty setting.
physician-assistants.tldr: PAs perform clinical and procedural work comparable to physicians within their specialty, but generic disability policies often undervalue your role by defining disability around physician income or supervisory functions rather than your actual clinical duties. Own-occupation coverage secures full benefits when disability prevents your specific clinical and procedural scope of practice, not your employer's supervisory requirements.

physicians.title: Physician Disability Insurance
physicians.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in physician disability insurance. All five major carriers compared, with each carrier's own-occupation definition and specialty recognition reviewed for physicians and surgeons.
physicians.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places physician coverage across all five major carriers, with every quote evaluated against occupation class, own-occupation contract language and specialty recognition, rider structure, and premium.

product-managers.title: Disability Insurance for Product Managers | Own-Occupation for a Judgment Role
product-managers.description: Disability insurance for tech product managers. The central issue is the own-occupation definition: a role defined by judgment and decision-making is harder to pin down at claim time, so a true own-occupation contract that measures disability against the actual PM job is what protects the income. Top 6A class, all five carriers compared.
product-managers.tldr: A product manager's value is judgment, strategy, and cross-functional leadership, not a measurable physical or coding output. That makes the own-occupation definition the decision that matters most: a role defined by decision-making is harder to pin down at claim time, so a true own-occupation contract that measures disability against the actual PM job is what keeps the income protected. Product managers also sit in a top occupation class (6A), and an individual policy stays portable across the job and startup moves a product career runs on. We compare all five major carriers on contract language and price.

professionals.title: Professional Disability Insurance
professionals.description: Seaworthy Insurance places disability insurance for licensed and credentialed professionals. All five major carriers compared on own-occupation language and occupation class, which varies widely across this group.
professionals.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places coverage for licensed and credentialed professionals across all five major carriers, evaluating own-occupation language, the occupation class each carrier assigns, and premium. Occupation class varies widely across this group, which is why a current quote across carriers is the only reliable read.

prosthodontists.title: Prosthodontist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
prosthodontists.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for prosthodontists. Protect your income against carpal tunnel from precision crown work, cervical disc disease from extended procedures, and hand tremor that compromises margin accuracy in implant restorations.
prosthodontists.tldr: Prosthodontists require exceptional fine motor precision for complex prosthodontic procedures including implant prosthetics, precision removable prosthetics, and complex laboratory coordination. Carpal tunnel, hand tremor, arthritis affecting fine motor dexterity, and back strain from sustained positioning is career-ending. Own-occupation coverage secures full benefits when hand or musculoskeletal disability prevents the specialized prosthodontic work your specialty income depends on.

psychiatrists.title: Psychiatrist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
psychiatrists.description: Disability insurance for psychiatrists, the specialty where full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage matters most and psychiatrists can hold it rather than the 24-month cap. Ameritas classes psychiatry a full tier above its peers at 5M, and true own-occupation protects your practice even though an MD can work elsewhere.
psychiatrists.tldr: Psychiatry is the specialty where the mental and nervous election matters most, because the category that most often ends a psychiatrist's career is the same one their patients carry, and psychiatrists are not in the group forced into the 24-month cap, so full-benefit-period coverage is available. The other two decisions that move the outcome are carrier class, where Ameritas is the standout at 5M against 4M or 4P everywhere else, and the definition of disability, since an MD who can no longer practice psychiatry can often still do administrative or research work, and only a true own-occupation contract keeps paying through that.

radiologists.title: Radiologist Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
radiologists.description: Disability insurance for radiologists. Diagnostic radiology classes well while interventional radiology classes lower, and the split drives your premium. Radiology earns preferred-occupation discounts at both Guardian and The Standard, and because a radiologist's income rides on reading images, vision and cognition are the career-ending risks a true own-occupation contract must cover.
radiologists.tldr: Radiology prices like two specialties, since diagnostic radiology classes as a favorable non-procedural specialty while interventional classes lower for its procedural and radiation exposure, and which one you are can move the premium a full tier. It is also one of the few specialties that earns a preferred-occupation discount at two carriers, Guardian and The Standard, which makes it inexpensive to insure per dollar of benefit. Because a radiologist's whole income rides on reading images, a vision or cognitive condition is the career-ending risk, so a true own-occupation definition and correct benefit sizing are the decisions that matter.

residents.title: Disability Insurance for Medical Residents and Fellows
residents.description: Why residents and fellows should lock in individual disability coverage during training: clean-record underwriting, a Future Increase Option, resident discounts, and the gaps in GME group plans.
residents.tldr: Training is the right time to put an individual disability policy in place, but not for the reason most marketing claims. The durable advantages are health and age (you are rated on a clean record before income rises), a Future Increase Option that locks insurability before any health or exclusion event, and portability the GME group plan does not give you. Real resident discounts exist (carrier programs commonly reaching 20% for medical residents and 10% for dental residents, plus general AMA and institutional programs), but the bigger lever is applying before any condition lands on your chart.

software-engineers.title: Disability Insurance for Software Engineers: RSI & Own-Occupation
software-engineers.description: Software engineers are the one tech role where hands-on injury is a real claim driver. Own-occupation coverage that protects against repetitive strain, carpal tunnel, and tendinopathy, written so a carrier cannot deny a claim just because you can still type. Class 6A pricing, all five carriers compared.
software-engineers.tldr: Software engineers are the one tech role where physical, hands-on risk is a genuine claim driver: years of sustained keyboard and mouse use commonly lead to repetitive strain injury, carpal tunnel, and tendinopathy in the exact hands the job runs on. That makes the own-occupation definition the decision that matters most. An any-occupation contract lets a carrier argue that an engineer who can still type is not disabled, which ignores the gap between basic computer use and professional engineering. Engineers sit in occupation class 6A and are usually straightforward to place well; we run all five major carriers on every case.

software-sales.title: Disability Insurance for Tech Sales | Coverage Sized to OTE
software-sales.description: Disability insurance for software and tech sales professionals: account executives, sales engineers, and account managers. Why group coverage insures base only and misses most of your on-target earnings, how carriers count and average commission, and why portability matters when you change companies often. All five carriers compared.
software-sales.tldr: Tech sales pay is mostly variable: base salary plus commission against an on-target-earnings (OTE) number, often with commission running half or more of the total. The problem that defines this role is that group long-term disability insures base salary only, so it protects a fraction of what a rep actually earns. An individual policy can be sized to total OTE because commission is earned income, which carriers count and average over about two years. It also stays with you through the frequent job changes a sales career brings. We run all five major carriers on every case.

sports-medicine.title: Sports Medicine Disability Insurance | Own-Occupation Coverage
sports-medicine.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance for sports medicine physicians. Protect your income against repetitive strain from ultrasound-guided procedures, musculoskeletal injury from high-volume exams, and sideline trauma exposure.
sports-medicine.tldr: Sports medicine physicians face high-volume musculoskeletal examination demands plus sideline coverage exposure. Own-occupation coverage secures protection if shoulder, wrist, or ankle injury; occupational arthritis; or overuse syndrome prevents ultrasound-guided procedures, even if you could do non-procedural sports medicine or telemedicine work.

surgeons.title: Disability Insurance for Surgeons | Own-Occupation Coverage
surgeons.description: Compare own-occupation disability insurance quotes for surgeons. Protect your income against hand tremor, cervical disc disease from OR posture, and needle stick exposure. See how carriers define disability for operative vs. non-operative work.
surgeons.tldr: Surgeons require true own-occupation coverage that protects against hand tremor, vision loss, and back injury that prevent operative work, even though you could theoretically do consultative or non-operative work. Own-occupation definition makes sure you're covered for inability to operate, not just inability to practice medicine.

tech.title: Tech Disability Insurance
tech.description: Seaworthy Insurance places disability insurance for software engineers, developers, tech sales, product managers, and data professionals. All five top carriers compared on occupation class, own-occupation language, mental-health treatment, and price.
tech.tldr: Seaworthy Insurance places tech coverage across all five major carriers, with every quote evaluated against occupation class, own-occupation contract language, how the benefit is sized to equity-heavy pay, and premium.

aana-disability-plan.title: The AANA Disability Plan for CRNAs: What It Covers and Where It Falls Short
aana-disability-plan.description: The AANA Member Advantage disability plan from New York Life: what it covers, the $12,000 cap, the 12-month mental-health limit, age-banded premiums, and where a high-earning CRNA needs an individual policy instead.
aana-disability-plan.tldr: The AANA Member Advantage plan is a member-paid group disability plan from New York Life. Premiums are age-banded and rise as you age, where an individual non-cancelable policy locks the rate to 65. It caps benefits at $12,000 a month (and at 70% of income, under a $20,000 aggregate), pays residual only after a prior period of total disability, limits mental/nervous and substance claims to 12 months, and reduces income earned in another occupation by 50%. Coverage is tied to AANA membership and ends by age 70. For a high-earning CRNA, an individual true own-occupation policy carries a higher benefit, residual on income loss alone, a longer mental/nervous benefit, and a premium fixed for the life of the contract.

business-finance-compensation.title: Disability Insurance for Variable, Equity, and Partnership Compensation
business-finance-compensation.description: How disability carriers size a benefit to total earned income for business and finance professionals paid in bonus, commission, partnership draws, K-1 income, and equity. What counts (base, bonus, commission, K-1 earned income, vested RSUs as W-2 wages when documented and recurring), what does not (unvested grants, options, ESPP discount, investment income), and how it is documented.
business-finance-compensation.tldr: Disability carriers size a benefit to your earned income, so for a business or finance professional the goal is a benefit built on total earned compensation rather than base salary. Base, bonus, and commission or on-target earnings are counted directly, with bonus and commission usually averaged over about two years. Partnership draws and K-1 earned income count for partners and owners. Vested RSUs are reported as W-2 wages, so that income generally counts when you can document a consistent vesting history. What does not count is contingent or unearned: unvested RSUs, unexercised stock options, the ESPP discount, and investment income such as dividends and capital gains. Documentation is about two years of tax returns plus K-1s, partnership statements, and vesting records. Group LTD almost always figures on base alone, which is why an individual policy usually carries the weight of protecting variable pay.

business-finance-group-vs-individual.title: Group vs. Individual Disability Insurance for Business and Finance Professionals
business-finance-group-vs-individual.description: Why employer group LTD underinsures executives, finance professionals, attorneys, and business owners: it figures on base salary only, caps the monthly benefit at $10,000 to $15,000, pays a taxable benefit when the employer funds it, switches to any-occupation after about 24 months, and ends when you leave. How an individual own-occupation policy fills the gap for bonus-, commission-, and partnership-weighted pay.
business-finance-group-vs-individual.tldr: Employer group long-term disability is the default coverage most business and finance professionals already have, and its structure underinsures them. It figures the benefit on base salary alone, so bonus, commission, partnership draws, K-1 earned income, and deferred compensation sit outside it. It commonly caps the monthly benefit at $10,000 to $15,000, pays a taxable benefit when the employer funds the premium, applies an own-occupation test that usually lasts about 24 months before switching to a stricter any-occupation standard, and ends the day you leave. Because pay in these fields is weighted toward variable and ownership income, a base-only group benefit protects a fraction of total earnings. An individual own-occupation policy is portable, pays its stated benefit regardless of other coverage, and can be sized to total earned income. Most professionals keep both, with the individual policy carrying the core weight.

business-finance-own-occupation.title: Own-Occupation Disability Insurance for Business and Finance Professionals
business-finance-own-occupation.description: True own-occupation is the provision that decides whether a disabled executive, business owner, attorney, financial professional, consultant, or accountant keeps their benefit. The 'you could still do some office work' trap, what a true own-occ definition protects for a high-skill role, and how the five major carriers handle these professions.
business-finance-own-occupation.tldr: For an executive, business owner, attorney, financial professional, consultant, or accountant, the own-occupation definition decides whether a claim pays. A true own-occupation contract pays if you cannot perform the material and substantial duties of your own occupation, even if you go on to work and earn in another field. A weaker any-occupation or modified definition lets a carrier argue that a disabled fund manager or executive could still do some general office work, and cut the benefit on that basis. What decides a claim is the definition type you bought plus the duties of the occupation you were actually performing when disability begins. Most office-based business and finance roles qualify for class 6A, one of the most favorable occupation classes, and all five major carriers write true own-occupation coverage for these professions.

business-finance-questions-before-buying.title: Questions Executives, Owners, and Attorneys Should Ask Before Buying Disability Insurance
business-finance-questions-before-buying.description: Before buying disability insurance as an executive, business owner, attorney, or financial professional, confirm true own-occupation for your actual role, a benefit sized to total earned income rather than base salary, business overhead expense or buy-sell coverage if you own the firm, a residual rider, a future-increase option, and a noncancelable contract.
business-finance-questions-before-buying.tldr: Before a business or finance professional buys disability insurance, a short list of provisions decides whether the policy fits. Is the definition true own-occupation for your actual role, so a litigator is protected as a litigator and a fund manager as a fund manager, not pushed into any office job? The Standard deems trial attorney a specialty under its Own Occupation Rider, which helps litigators. Is the benefit sized to your total earned income, including bonus, commission, partnership draws and K-1 earnings, deferred compensation, and vested equity, rather than base salary alone? If you own the business, do you also need Business Overhead Expense, buy-sell, or key-person coverage on top of personal income protection? Is a residual rider included for partial losses, and a future-increase option so coverage grows with income? Are you applying at the cleanest underwriting window, while the health record is clean? Is the policy noncancelable so the carrier cannot raise your premium or change terms? Run all of it across all five major carriers on contract language, not price, because the answers differ by carrier.

business-finance-quote-comparison.title: Disability Insurance Quote Comparison for Business and Finance Professionals
business-finance-quote-comparison.description: How the five major disability carriers compare for executives, business owners, attorneys, financial professionals, consultants, and accountants on contract language. Own-occupation mechanism, occupation class, and the standout feature for each of Guardian, MassMutual, The Standard, Ameritas, and Principal, plus why comparing definition wording matters more than price.
business-finance-quote-comparison.tldr: All five major disability carriers can be written as true own-occupation for business and finance professionals, and most office-based roles in this group qualify for class 6A, one of the most favorable occupation classes. How each carrier delivers the own-occupation definition differs: Guardian and Ameritas in the base contract, MassMutual via its Own Occupation Rider, Principal through its own-occupation definition as placed, and The Standard through a rider that also deems 'trial attorney' a specialty for litigators. Standouts worth knowing: Ameritas carries the highest business overhead expense limit of the majors at $100,000 a month for owners, and Principal is the most flexible on underwriting. Because the definitions are not interchangeable, the comparison worth making is on contract wording, not price alone.

crna-ameritas.title: Ameritas Disability Insurance for CRNAs
crna-ameritas.description: How Ameritas's DInamic Cornerstone treats a CRNA: true own-occupation in the base contract, the 24-month mental health limitation with a neurocognitive carve-out, the 2026 exam waiver for applicants 50 and under, and where Ameritas fits.
crna-ameritas.tldr: Ameritas writes CRNAs through its DInamic Cornerstone policy (form 4601NC) with true own-occupation built into the base definition, no rider required. It classes a nurse anesthetist at 3M, the same tier as Guardian and a notch below MassMutual's 4A, so MassMutual usually prices lower for a CRNA. A nurse anesthetist's mental health and substance claims pay for at most 24 months, the cap shared across the majors, though Ameritas pays neurocognitive conditions like dementia as ordinary sickness outside it. The carrier holds an A from AM Best with a Comdex of 82 as of 2026 and in our experience underwrites toward the conservative end, which makes it strongest on clean files.

crna-disability-insurance-by-career-stag.title: CRNA Disability Insurance by Career Stage: New Graduate to Retirement
crna-disability-insurance-by-career-stag.description: How the right disability coverage decision changes for a CRNA across career stages: locking in early as a new graduate, closing the underinsurance gap mid-career, and matching coverage to the retirement timeline.
crna-disability-insurance-by-career-stag.tldr: The right disability decision for a CRNA changes with career stage. New graduates should lock in coverage during the clean-underwriting window and use future increase options to scale it. Mid-career CRNAs need to close the gap between a policy sized to a starting salary and current income, before accumulated wear is documented and complicates re-underwriting. CRNAs approaching retirement should match the benefit period to their planned retirement age and watch for an occupation-definition mismatch if they move into non-clinical work.

crna-disability-insurance-cost.title: How Much Disability Insurance Costs for CRNAs
crna-disability-insurance-cost.description: What CRNAs pay for individual disability insurance, drawn from Seaworthy's placed book: most policies land between roughly $225 and $430 per month, typically 1% to 2.5% of income. Age, occupation class, benefit amount, elimination period, and riders drive the price.
crna-disability-insurance-cost.tldr: Across the CRNA policies in Seaworthy's placed book, as of the 2026 review, most premiums land between roughly $225 and $430 per month, with the median near $300, typically 1% to 2.5% of income. The biggest lever is age at purchase: measured per $1,000 of monthly benefit, the cost nearly doubles between buyers in their late 20s and buyers past 50. Health is the other, since about 4 in 10 CRNA applications in our book draw an exclusion or a rating (2026 audit).

crna-disability-insurance-mistakes.title: 7 Disability Insurance Mistakes CRNAs Make Before Mid-Career
crna-disability-insurance-mistakes.description: The common gaps in CRNA disability coverage before they become claims: relying on group LTD alone, an any-occupation definition, skipped riders, inflation exposure, and bad timing. What each costs and how to fix it.
crna-disability-insurance-mistakes.tldr: Common CRNA coverage gaps include relying on hospital group coverage alone, accepting an any-occupation definition, skipping the residual rider that protects partial-disability claims, and leaving off the cost-of-living rider on a long claim. Each leaves a high earner under-protected, and nearly all of them are settled at application, long before a claim is ever filed.

crna-disability-risks.title: CRNA Disability Risks and How Disability Coverage Responds
crna-disability-risks.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in CRNA coverage. The disability risks CRNAs face most, from musculoskeletal injury to mental health and substance use, and how the policy definition and limitations decide each claim.
crna-disability-risks.tldr: The disability risks most likely to interrupt or end a CRNA's career fall into four categories: musculoskeletal injury, mental health and burnout, substance use disorder, and hand or nerve conditions. Whether a claim pays turns on a few policy-level details: a true own-occupation definition measured against your actual anesthesia duties, a benefit period long enough for multi-year conditions, and the mental and nervous limitation that commonly caps psychiatric claims at 24 months.

crna-group-vs-individual.title: CRNA Group vs Individual Disability Insurance: Why Hospital Coverage Falls Short
crna-group-vs-individual.description: CRNA group LTD plans commonly cap benefits at $10,000 to $15,000/mo, pay taxable benefits, provide only time-limited own-occupation protection, and end at job change. Individual coverage closes the after-tax gap.
crna-group-vs-individual.tldr: Hospital group LTD plans for CRNAs commonly cap benefits around $10,000 per month, and because employer-paid group benefits are generally taxable, a stated $10,000 benefit typically nets closer to $6,500 after tax. An individual policy is paid tax-free and can be written as true own-occupation, so the after-tax benefit an individual policy can add is often several thousand dollars per month even when the face-value figures look close.

crna-guardian.title: Guardian Disability Insurance for CRNAs
crna-guardian.description: How Guardian's Provider Choice policy treats a CRNA: the 3M occupation class, true own-occupation in the base contract, the required 24-month mental health limitation, and where Guardian fits against the other major carriers.
crna-guardian.tldr: Guardian writes CRNAs through its Provider Choice policy (form 18ID, issued by Berkshire Life) at occupation class 3M, with true own-occupation built into the base contract. Mental health and substance claims are limited to 24 months for a nurse anesthetist, as they are at every major carrier. Guardian carries the highest financial-strength marks of the five majors, A++ from AM Best with a Comdex of 100 as of 2026, and in our experience the most conservative underwriting of the group. It tends to fit CRNAs with clean health histories who want the strongest contract; a complicated file often gets a better outcome elsewhere.

crna-massmutual.title: MassMutual Disability Insurance for CRNAs
crna-massmutual.description: How MassMutual's Radius Choice treats a CRNA: the 4A occupation class upgraded from 3A in 2024, true own-occupation through the Own Occupation Rider, the 24-month mental health limitation, and where MassMutual fits among the majors.
crna-massmutual.tldr: MassMutual writes CRNAs through its Radius Choice policy (form ICC15-XLIS-RC) at occupation class 4A, a public upgrade from 3A in 2024 that improved how the company prices nurse anesthetists. True own-occupation protection comes through the Own Occupation Rider, which must be added at purchase. A CRNA's mental health and substance claims pay benefits for 24 months at most, the cap every major applies to the profession. MassMutual pairs an A++ from AM Best and a Comdex of 98 as of 2026 with participating policies that can be credited dividends, and in our experience its underwriting sits in the middle of the five majors.

crna-own-occupation.title: How Own-Occupation Definitions Affect CRNA Disability Claims
crna-own-occupation.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in CRNA own-occupation coverage. A CRNA's claim is decided by a true own-occupation definition applied to anesthesia work; correct classification and documented income at underwriting set the occupation class, premium, and benefit size.
crna-own-occupation.tldr: Own-occupation is the provision that decides a CRNA disability claim. The major carriers do not name anesthesia in the contract; each measures disability against the material and substantial duties of your occupation at the time disability begins, which for a working CRNA is the delivery of anesthesia. A true own-occupation definition keeps paying total-disability benefits even if you can no longer give anesthesia but work in another occupation. Being underwritten and classified as a nurse anesthetist, with full CRNA income documented, still matters, but it sets your occupation class, premium, and benefit size, not the standard the claim is judged by. The main risk to watch is an any-occupation definition, settled before you ever file a claim.

crna-practice-settings.title: CRNA Practice Settings and How Each Shapes Disability Coverage
crna-practice-settings.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in CRNA coverage. Hospital, anesthesia group, independent contractor, and locum tenens work each drive different income documentation and policy provision requirements.
crna-practice-settings.tldr: Where and how you practice anesthesia directly shapes what a disability policy needs to cover. Hospital-employed CRNAs, anesthesia group members, independent contractors, and locum tenens providers each face different income documentation realities, occupational definition considerations, and portability concerns. Structuring coverage around the actual practice setting prevents gaps that surface only at claim time.

crna-principal.title: Principal Disability Insurance for CRNAs
crna-principal.description: How Principal's Income Protector treats a CRNA: the 2M+ occupation class, the True Own Occupation definition Seaworthy quotes, the 24-month mental health limitation, and the underwriting flexibility that makes Principal the carrier for complicated files.
crna-principal.tldr: Principal writes CRNAs through its Income Protector policy (form ICC22-800) at occupation class 2M+, and every Principal quote Seaworthy runs uses the True Own Occupation definition, so a CRNA's claim is measured against anesthesia work even if other employment follows. The 24-month limitation on mental health and substance claims applies to nurse anesthetists here as it does at all five majors. Principal carries an A+ from AM Best with a Comdex of 90 as of 2026, and in our experience it is the most flexible underwriter of the group, which makes it the first carrier we test when a CRNA's medical or income history needs to be argued.

crna-questions-before-buying.title: 8 Questions Every CRNA Should Ask Before Buying Disability Insurance
crna-questions-before-buying.description: Seaworthy Insurance outlines eight questions CRNAs should ask before buying disability coverage, from the own-occupation definition to occupation class, residual activation, and underwriting, so you know how a policy pays before you need it.
crna-questions-before-buying.tldr: The premium and the monthly benefit are the easy parts of a CRNA disability policy. What decides whether a claim pays is the definition of disability, the occupation class, the riders, and how the policy was underwritten. These eight questions cover each of those before you buy, while you can still change the answer.

crna-the-standard.title: The Standard Disability Insurance for CRNAs
crna-the-standard.description: How The Standard's Platinum Advantage treats a CRNA: the 2P occupation class, why the Own Occupation Rider is unavailable at that class, what the Regular Occupation base definition pays, and where The Standard still fits.
crna-the-standard.tldr: The Standard writes CRNAs through its Platinum Advantage policy at occupation class 2P, and at that class its Own Occupation Rider is unavailable, so a CRNA's policy with The Standard is not true own-occupation. The base Regular Occupation definition pays full total-disability benefits while a disabled CRNA is not working in another occupation, and residual coverage pays on partial income loss at a 20% threshold, higher than the 15% trigger at the other majors. Mental health and substance claims are limited to 24 months, as at all five carriers. The Standard holds an A from AM Best with a Comdex of 84 as of 2026, and in our experience is the second most flexible underwriter of the group.

crna-underwriting.title: CRNA Disability Insurance Underwriting: What to Expect
crna-underwriting.description: Seaworthy Insurance specializes in CRNA coverage. What disability insurance underwriting asks a CRNA for, the rating and exclusion triggers specific to the profession, and why roughly 40% of placed CRNA policies come back modified.
crna-underwriting.tldr: Underwriting a CRNA disability policy runs on two files: your medical record and your income documentation. Roughly 40% of the CRNA policies in Seaworthy's placed book carry an exclusion or a premium rating per the 2026 audit, and about half of those exclusions are for mental and nervous conditions, with back and neck history the other recurring driver. A modified offer is still a placed policy, and because an individual application can be shopped across five carriers at once, where and when you apply moves the outcome more than anything else you control.

dentist-business-overhead-expense.title: Business Overhead Expense Insurance for Practice-Owner Dentists
dentist-business-overhead-expense.description: Business overhead expense insurance reimburses a dental practice's fixed costs, staff salaries, rent, and equipment loans, while the owner is disabled, so the practice survives. It is separate from a personal own-occupation policy, which replaces the dentist's income; practice owners generally need both.
dentist-business-overhead-expense.tldr: Business overhead expense (BOE) insurance is built for a practice-owner dentist who is disabled and cannot generate revenue but still owes the practice's fixed bills. It reimburses covered costs such as staff salaries, rent, equipment and practice loans, and utilities, typically for a limited period of 12 to 24 months, so the practice can stay open or be sold rather than collapse. BOE is a different product from a personal own-occupation policy: BOE keeps the business running, while the personal policy replaces the dentist's own income. The two cover different bills and are sized separately. Among the carriers Seaworthy places, Ameritas offers one of the highest BOE monthly limits at $100,000, while The Standard offers BOE through a separate Business Overhead Protector product. A practice owner generally needs both a personal own-occupation policy and BOE; either one alone leaves a gap.

dentist-disability-risks.title: Dentist Disability Risks and Why Own-Occupation Coverage Matters
dentist-disability-risks.description: Dentistry is fine-motor, hands-on work. The disability risks dentists face most, from hand and wrist conditions to neck and back musculoskeletal injury, vision, and mental health, and why a true own-occupation definition paired with residual coverage decides each claim.
dentist-disability-risks.tldr: Dentistry depends on fine motor control and a sustained, physically awkward posture, so the disability risks most likely to end a dentist's clinical career concentrate in the hands and wrists, the neck and back, the eyes, and mental health. A small loss of fine-motor control can end clinical dentistry while leaving other work possible, which is exactly the situation a true own-occupation definition is built to cover, with a residual rider handling the partial-disability claims that are more common than total disability.

dentist-group-vs-individual.title: Dentist Group vs Individual Disability Insurance: Why Individual Coverage Is the Core
dentist-group-vs-individual.description: Most dentists are practice owners or associates with little or no employer group LTD, so individual own-occupation coverage is the core protection, not a supplement. Group plans cap benefits, cover base salary only, are taxable when employer-paid, and end at a job change.
dentist-group-vs-individual.tldr: Most dentists work as practice owners or associates and have little or no employer-provided long-term disability coverage, so for a dentist an individual own-occupation policy is the foundation rather than a top-up on a group plan. Where group coverage does exist it tends to cap the benefit at $10,000 to $15,000 a month, cover base salary only, pay taxable benefits when the employer funds the premium, limit own-occupation protection to roughly 24 months, and end the day employment ends. An individual policy is owned by the dentist, travels across the associate-to-owner transition, and can be written as true own-occupation that protects clinical dental work.

dentist-own-occupation.title: Why a Dentist Needs True Own-Occupation Disability Insurance
dentist-own-occupation.description: Seaworthy places dentist own-occupation coverage across all five major carriers. A weak definition lets a carrier argue a hand-injured dentist could do general dentistry, consulting, or teaching and cut the benefit; true specialty own-occupation ties the claim to the dental work you actually do.
dentist-own-occupation.tldr: True own-occupation is the provision that decides a dentist's disability claim. A weak or any-occupation contract lets a carrier argue that a hand-injured periodontist could still do general dentistry, consult, or teach, and reduce or deny the benefit on that basis. A true own-occupation definition keeps paying total-disability benefits when you can no longer do your dental work, even if you take other work. For sub-specialists, specialty deeming matters: a carrier that recognizes your ADA specialty as your occupation measures the claim against that specialty rather than against dentistry in general. All five major carriers can be written true own-occupation for a dentist. How each carrier gets there differs, which is why the definition and the classification both belong in writing before you buy.

dentist-questions-before-buying.title: Questions a Dentist Should Ask Before Buying Disability Insurance
dentist-questions-before-buying.description: Seaworthy places dentist disability coverage across all five major carriers. Before you buy, confirm true specialty own-occupation for your ADA specialty, a residual rider at a 15-20% threshold, mental and nervous coverage where available, business overhead expense if you own the practice, a benefit-increase option, and whether to apply while young and healthy.
dentist-questions-before-buying.tldr: Before a dentist buys disability insurance, six questions decide whether the policy fits. Is the definition true specialty own-occupation for your ADA specialty, so the claim is measured against your dental work? Is a residual rider included at a 15 to 20 percent income-loss threshold for partial claims? Is full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage available, and worth the cost, given how those conditions drive claims? Does business overhead expense cover the practice's fixed costs if you own it? Is a benefit-increase option in place so coverage can grow with income? And does applying young, while the health record is clean, make sense, given that the dentist median age at issue is the youngest of the major professions? Run all six across all five major carriers, because the answers differ by carrier.

dentist-quote-comparison.title: Dentist Disability Insurance: Comparing the Five Major Carriers
dentist-quote-comparison.description: All five major disability carriers, The Standard, Guardian, MassMutual, Ameritas, and Principal, can be written as true own-occupation for dentists. They differ in how they deliver it, how they class dental specialties, and where each one stands out, which is what a side-by-side comparison is for.
dentist-quote-comparison.tldr: For a dentist, the five major disability carriers, The Standard, Guardian, MassMutual, Ameritas, and Principal, can each be written as true own-occupation, so the comparison is about contract language and fit, not just price. They deliver own-occupation differently: The Standard through its Own Occupation Rider for class 3D with ADA-specialty deeming, Guardian through Specialty Own-Occupation for dental classes, MassMutual through recognition of an ADA billing-code specialty, and Ameritas and Principal in the base definition. Each has a standout for dentists: Ameritas the highest BOE limit, MassMutual a 3D-to-4D upgrade with an AEGD or GPR residency plus a dental resident discount, The Standard a Residency Multi-Life Discount, Principal the most flexible underwriting of the five. Because the same dentist can be classed and priced differently from one carrier to the next, the right answer comes from running all five side by side.

physician-benefit-sizing.title: How Much Disability Insurance Can a Physician Get? Benefit Sizing Explained
physician-benefit-sizing.description: Carriers set a maximum dollar benefit from documented income through issue and participation limits, not a flat 60 percent. A single carrier will typically issue up to about $20,000 a month, varying by income, state, and specialty, with larger totals sometimes possible across carriers. Self-funded benefits are tax-free.
physician-benefit-sizing.tldr: How much disability coverage a physician can secure is set by carrier issue and participation limits, which convert documented income into a maximum dollar benefit rather than a flat percentage of pay. The most a single carrier will typically issue for a high earner is about $20,000 a month, varying by income, state, and specialty, and larger totals are sometimes possible by combining carriers. The replacement percentage declines as income rises, so the flat 60 percent rule of thumb does not hold for physician incomes, and because the maximum can sit below full income, the definition of disability and the residual rider decide how much of that income the policy actually protects. A future-increase feature locks in the right to raise coverage as income grows without new medical underwriting, which matters most for residents and fellows applying before their attending income arrives.

physician-disability-risks.title: Physician Disability Risks by Specialty and Why the Definition Decides
physician-disability-risks.description: Physician disability risk is specialty-dependent. The major categories are procedural and fine-motor loss for surgeons and proceduralists, mental health and burnout, musculoskeletal injury, and cognitive or neurological conditions. Why a hand or back condition can end operating while other medicine remains possible, and how the own-occupation definition decides each claim.
physician-disability-risks.tldr: Physician disability risk depends heavily on specialty. The major categories are procedural and fine-motor loss that ends operating for surgeons and proceduralists, mental health and burnout, musculoskeletal injury, and cognitive or neurological conditions. The defining feature for many physicians is that a single hand or back condition can end a procedural career while leaving other medicine fully possible, which is exactly the situation a true own-occupation definition is built to cover, paired with residual coverage for the partial-disability claims that are more common than total disability.

physician-group-vs-individual.title: Physician Group vs Individual Disability Insurance: Why Group LTD Falls Short
physician-group-vs-individual.description: Employed and hospital-based physicians often have group long-term disability, but it caps the benefit at $10,000 to $15,000 a month, counts base salary only, is taxable when the employer pays, switches to an any-occupation test after about 24 months, and ends at a job change. Individual own-occupation coverage is the portable, tax-free core.
physician-group-vs-individual.tldr: Many employed and hospital-based physicians have group long-term disability through their employer, but for a high-earning physician it tends to fall short in five specific ways. Group LTD commonly caps the benefit at $10,000 to $15,000 a month, figures on base salary only (so it excludes call pay, bonus, RVU and productivity compensation, and partnership distributions), pays taxable benefits when the employer funds the premium, limits own-occupation protection to roughly the first 24 months of a claim before switching to an any-occupation test, and ends the day employment ends. An individual policy is owned by the physician, sized to total documented income, paid tax-free when self-funded, and can be written as true own-occupation that protects the physician's specialty, so it is the portable core of income protection rather than a supplement on top of group.

physician-mental-health.title: Physician Mental Health Disability Coverage and the 24-Month Cap
physician-mental-health.description: Most physicians can secure full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage, not the 24-month cap. The cap is forced only on a defined high-risk group: anesthesiology, emergency medicine, pain management, nurse anesthetists, and general dentistry. How each major carrier delivers full-period mental health coverage for everyone else, with CA and NY caveats.
physician-mental-health.tldr: The 24-month mental and nervous limitation that caps psychiatric and burnout claims is not universal for physicians. It is forced only on a defined high-risk group, anesthesiology, emergency medicine, pain management, nurse anesthetists, and general dentistry. Surgeons are not in that group, and most office-based and specialist physicians are not either, so for the majority of physicians full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage is available. How it is delivered varies by carrier, and California and New York carry their own caveats.

physician-occupation-classes.title: Physician Occupation Classes: How the Five Major Carriers Class Your Specialty
physician-occupation-classes.description: The same physician specialty is classed very differently across Guardian, Principal, MassMutual, Ameritas, and The Standard, and class is a primary driver of premium. The full specialty-by-specialty grid, compiled from the carriers' current producer guides.
physician-occupation-classes.tldr: Disability carriers assign every physician specialty an occupation class, and the class is a primary driver of what you pay. The assignments diverge sharply: an orthopedic surgeon is classed 5M at Ameritas but 3M at Guardian and Principal, a psychiatrist is a full class apart between Ameritas and Guardian, and a pediatrician is Principal's only top-class physician. No single carrier classes every specialty favorably, which is why the same physician can see materially different premiums across the five majors. Classes are revised periodically; a current quote run at all five carriers is the only reliable read.

physician-own-occupation.title: Why a Physician Needs True Own-Occupation Disability Insurance
physician-own-occupation.description: A weak own-occupation definition lets a carrier argue a hand-injured surgeon could practice non-procedural medicine and cut the benefit; true specialty own-occupation ties the claim to the work you actually do, including the surgical procedures that drive a proceduralist's income. Compared across all five major carriers.
physician-own-occupation.tldr: True own-occupation is the provision that decides a physician's disability claim. A weak or any-occupation contract lets a carrier argue that a hand-injured surgeon could still see patients, read studies, or move into non-procedural medicine, and reduce or deny the benefit on that basis. A true own-occupation definition keeps paying total-disability benefits when you can no longer do your medical work, even if you take other work. For proceduralists, specialty recognition matters most: Guardian's Enhanced Medical Specialty definition deems a surgeon who earns most income from surgical procedures totally disabled if a condition ends those procedures, even while working in another role; MassMutual recognizes the specialty verified by your CPT billing codes; The Standard deems an ABMS or AOABOS specialty your occupation. All five major carriers can be written true own-occupation for a physician. How each carrier gets there differs, which is why the definition and the classification both belong in writing before you buy.

physician-questions-before-buying.title: Questions a Physician Should Ask Before Buying Disability Insurance
physician-questions-before-buying.description: Seaworthy places physician disability coverage across all five major carriers. Before you buy, confirm true own-occupation with specialty recognition for your specialty, procedural-income protection if you operate, full-benefit-period mental and nervous coverage if you are not in the high-risk group, a residual rider at a 15-20% threshold, a future increase option to grow with income, and whether to apply at the cleanest underwriting window.
physician-questions-before-buying.tldr: Before a physician buys disability insurance, six questions decide whether the policy fits. Is the definition true own-occupation with specialty recognition for your specialty, so a claim is measured against your medical work? If you operate, does the definition protect your procedural income specifically, as Guardian's Enhanced MD/DO definition is built to do? Are you in the high-risk group forced into a 24-month mental and nervous cap, anesthesiology, emergency medicine, or pain management, or can you secure full-benefit-period coverage, which most physicians including surgeons can? Is a residual rider included at a 15 to 20 percent income-loss threshold? Is a future increase option in place so coverage can grow with income, which matters most for residents and fellows? And are you applying at the cleanest underwriting window, while the health record is clean? Run all six across all five major carriers, because the answers differ by carrier.

physician-quote-comparison.title: Physician Disability Insurance Quote Comparison: The Big 5 Compared
physician-quote-comparison.description: Seaworthy compares the five major disability carriers for a physician on contract language, not price.
