All five can be written true own-occupation; what differs is how each recognizes your specialty, the physician occupation classes, and the standout feature, from Guardian's Enhanced Medical Specialty surgical definition to MassMutual's CPT billing-code recognition.
physician-quote-comparison.tldr: All five major carriers we place can be written true own-occupation for a physician, so the comparison that matters is contract language, not price. Guardian writes true own-occupation in its base contract and adds an Enhanced Medical Specialty definition that ties a qualifying surgeon's claim to surgical procedures. MassMutual delivers it through its Own Occupation Rider with CPT billing-code specialty recognition. The Standard deems an ABMS or AOABOS specialty your occupation and adds the Own Occupation Rider, which physicians qualify for. Ameritas provides true own-occupation in its base definition. Principal provides true own-occupation as placed and is the most flexible of the five on underwriting. The right carrier depends on your specialty, income, state, and medical history, which is why every quote should be run across all five at once.

professionals-group-vs-individual.title: Group vs Individual Disability Insurance for Licensed and Credentialed Professionals
professionals-group-vs-individual.description: Why hospital, health-system, and firm group LTD leaves a gap for licensed and credentialed professionals. Benefit caps, base-salary-only coverage, taxability, the switch to an any-occupation test after about 24 months, and why an individual own-occupation policy is the portable core.
professionals-group-vs-individual.tldr: For a licensed or credentialed professional, hospital, health-system, or firm group long-term disability coverage is a useful floor but a weak foundation. Group LTD caps the benefit, usually figures on base salary only, becomes taxable when the employer pays the premium, and almost always switches from an own-occupation test to a much stricter any-occupation test after roughly 24 months. It also ends when you change jobs. An individual own-occupation policy is owned by you, moves with you, and is built to keep paying against the duties of your specific licensed or credentialed role. For most professionals in this group, the individual policy is the core and the group plan is the supplement on top.

professionals-occupation-class.title: Occupation Class for Licensed and Credentialed Professionals
professionals-occupation-class.description: Occupation class varies widely across licensed professionals, unlike physicians or finance pros who cluster at the top. What the class drives (own-occ availability, issue and participation caps, price) and what it does not decide (the claim, which turns on the definition type and your real duties). Allied-health constraints and favored technical office classes.
professionals-occupation-class.tldr: Occupation class is the carrier's risk tier for a job, and for licensed and credentialed professionals it varies widely, unlike physicians or finance professionals who cluster at the top. The class drives which definitions and riders are available, the issue and participation caps on your benefit, and your price. It does not decide a claim. The claim turns on the definition type you bought and the material and substantial duties of the occupation you were performing when disability begins. Allied-health roles can carry class-based constraints, such as the mandatory 24-month own-occupation limitation Principal applies to pharmacists, while favored technical office professions can earn advantages like The Standard's Preferred Occupation Discount of up to 20% for engineers. There is no single class for this group, which is exactly why a current quote across carriers is the only reliable read.

professionals-own-occupation.title: Own-Occupation Disability Insurance for Licensed and Credentialed Professionals
professionals-own-occupation.description: For a licensed or credentialed professional, the credential is the asset. True own-occupation protects the specific licensed role. The 'you could still do other work' any-occupation trap, why the definition type decides a claim, and why carrier selection matters for some allied-health roles.
professionals-own-occupation.tldr: For a licensed or credentialed professional, the credential or license is the asset, and the own-occupation definition decides whether a claim pays. A true own-occupation contract pays if you cannot perform the material and substantial duties of your own occupation, even if you go on to work and earn in another field. A weaker any-occupation or modified definition lets a carrier argue that a disabled pharmacist or engineer could still do some other work and cut the benefit on that basis. What decides a claim is the definition type you bought plus the duties of the occupation you were actually performing when disability begins, not the occupation-class label. All five major carriers write true own-occupation coverage for these professions, but the mechanism differs by carrier, and for some allied-health roles the carrier you pick changes what you can get.

professionals-questions-before-buying.title: Questions Licensed Professionals Should Ask Before Buying Disability Insurance
professionals-questions-before-buying.description: Before buying disability insurance as a licensed professional, confirm true own-occupation for your licensed role, learn the occupation class you will be assigned and whether it limits own-occupation, size the benefit to total income rather than base, and check for a residual rider, a future-increase option, and a clean underwriting window.
professionals-questions-before-buying.tldr: Before a licensed professional outside medicine, dentistry, law, and tech buys disability insurance, a short list of provisions decides whether the policy fits. Is the definition true own-occupation for your licensed role, not a modified or any-occupation contract that lets a carrier argue you could still do some other work? What occupation class will you be assigned, and does that class limit own-occupation? This is the question that varies most across this group: a pharmacist faces a mandatory 24-month own-occupation limitation at Principal, while a favored office profession like an engineer can earn The Standard's Preferred Occupation Discount of up to 20 percent. Is the benefit sized to your total income, not just base salary? Is a residual rider included for partial losses, and a future-increase option so coverage grows with income without new medical underwriting? And are you applying at the cleanest underwriting window, while the health record is clean? Run all of it across all five major carriers on contract language, not price, because the answers differ by carrier and by occupation class.

professionals-quote-comparison.title: Disability Insurance Quote Comparison for Licensed and Credentialed Professionals
professionals-quote-comparison.description: How the five major disability carriers compare for licensed and credentialed professionals on contract language. Own-occupation mechanism, occupation class range, and the standout for each of Guardian, MassMutual, The Standard, Ameritas, and Principal, including the mandatory 24-month own-occupation limitation for pharmacists at Principal.
professionals-quote-comparison.tldr: All five major disability carriers can be written as true own-occupation for licensed and credentialed professionals, but how they deliver it and what occupation class they assign varies widely across this group. Guardian and Ameritas build the true own-occupation definition into the base contract; MassMutual delivers it through its Own Occupation Rider and classes many of these roles at 4A; The Standard delivers it through a rider and offers a Preferred Occupation Discount of up to 20% for favored office professions including engineers; Principal places it as true own-occupation but applies a mandatory 24-month own-occupation limitation for pharmacists. Because this group spreads across the occupation-class scale, the class assigned drives availability, limits, and price, while the claim still turns on the definition type and your real duties. The comparison worth making is on contract wording, not price alone.

tech-disability-insurance-cost.title: How Much Disability Insurance Costs for Tech Workers
tech-disability-insurance-cost.description: What individual disability insurance costs for technology professionals and what drives the premium. Office-based tech sits in occupation class 6A, a top class that prices well. Age, health, benefit amount, elimination period, benefit period, and riders all move the price. Industry premiums commonly run roughly 1% to 3% of income.
tech-disability-insurance-cost.tldr: Tech is inexpensive to insure relative to the income it protects, because office-based technology roles sit in occupation class 6A, one of the top occupation classes carriers use. Low-hazard cognitive work prices well. As a general industry guideline, individual disability premiums commonly run roughly 1% to 3% of income, and the figure tracks age and health at application, occupation class, benefit amount, elimination period, benefit period, and rider selection. Buying early, while young and healthy, locks in the lowest rate and the best health class.

tech-group-vs-individual.title: Group vs. Individual Disability Insurance for Tech Workers
tech-group-vs-individual.description: Why employer group LTD underinsures tech professionals: it generally covers base salary only, caps the monthly benefit, pays a taxable benefit, switches to any-occupation after about 24 months, and ends when you leave. How an individual own-occupation policy fills the gap for equity- and bonus-heavy pay.
tech-group-vs-individual.tldr: Employer group long-term disability is the default coverage a tech worker has, and it has structural limits: it generally replaces about 60% of base salary only, commonly caps the monthly benefit at $10,000 to $15,000 for most employees, pays a taxable benefit when the employer funds the premium, applies an own-occupation test that commonly lasts about 24 months before switching to an any-occupation standard, and ends the day you leave the job. Because tech pay is weighted toward bonus and equity, a base-only group benefit protects a fraction of total compensation. An individual own-occupation policy is the fix: it pays its stated benefit regardless of other coverage, can be sized to total earned income, is portable across job changes, and locks in your rate and health class. Most tech workers keep both, with the individual policy carrying the core weight.

tech-h1b-visa.title: Disability Insurance for H-1B & Visa-Holding Tech Workers
tech-h1b-visa.description: Why individual disability insurance matters for technology workers on H-1B and other work visas. Group coverage ends when employment ends, which for a visa holder can coincide with a status problem. How carriers generally underwrite applicants on temporary work visas, how to size the benefit to total earned income, and why timing while employed and healthy matters.
tech-h1b-visa.tldr: For a technology worker on an H-1B or similar work visa, income protection carries a risk most US-born workers do not face: work-visa status is generally tied to employment, so a disability that ends your job can also threaten your status. An individual disability policy is owned by you and stays in force regardless of employer or status changes, while group long-term disability ends the day employment ends. All five major carriers we work with will consider applicants on H-1B and similar work visas, generally case-by-case, and green-card holders are typically underwritten on the same basis as US citizens. Terms differ by carrier, so running all five finds the best fit. Buying while employed, healthy, and authorized to work locks in coverage and rate, with technology occupations generally classified 6A, one of the most favorable classes.

tech-mental-health.title: Mental-Health & Burnout Disability Coverage for Tech Workers
tech-mental-health.description: Why most disability contracts cap mental and nervous claims at 24 months, why tech professionals are usually exempt from that limitation, and how applying before any treatment is on record keeps full-benefit-period mental-health coverage available.
tech-mental-health.tldr: Burnout, anxiety, and depression are among the most common reasons a tech professional would file a disability claim, yet most contracts cap mental and nervous claims at 24 months even when the policy otherwise pays to age 65. Tech professionals are usually exempt from that cap, so full-benefit-period mental-health coverage is available to them in a way it is not for some higher-risk medical specialties. It is available across the major carriers, by different mechanisms: by default at Guardian and Principal, as the standard option at Ameritas and The Standard, where the 24-month cap is only an optional discount, and by endorsement at MassMutual. The catch is timing: this coverage is only available before any mental-health treatment is on the record, which is the single strongest reason for a tech worker to apply early.

tech-own-occupation.title: Own-Occupation Disability Insurance for Tech Workers
tech-own-occupation.description: The own-occupation definition is the single provision that decides whether a tech professional's claim pays. The three definition types explained, the 'you can still use a computer' trap, and why the definition you bought and the duties of your occupation at the time of disability, not contract keywords, decide a claim.
tech-own-occupation.tldr: The own-occupation definition is the provision that decides whether a tech worker's disability claim pays. A true own-occupation contract pays if you cannot perform the material and substantial duties of your own occupation, even if you go on to work and earn in a different field. A modified or transitional definition stops paying once you work elsewhere, and an any-occupation definition pays only if you cannot work at all. What actually decides a claim is two things together: the definition type you bought, and the duties of the occupation you were actually performing when disability begins. Tech roles generally qualify for class 6A, one of the most favorable occupation classes, where true own-occupation coverage is available across the major carriers.

tech-rsu-equity-compensation.title: Disability Insurance for RSUs & Equity Compensation
tech-rsu-equity-compensation.description: How disability carriers treat RSUs, bonus, ESPP, and stock options when sizing a tech worker's benefit. Vested RSUs are W-2 wages and generally count when documented; unvested grants and options do not. What to document and how to size coverage to total compensation.
tech-rsu-equity-compensation.tldr: Disability carriers size a benefit to your earned income. Base salary, bonus, and commission are counted directly, with bonus and commission usually averaged over about two years. Vested RSUs are reported as W-2 wages, so that income generally counts when you can document a consistent vesting history. Unvested RSUs, unexercised stock options, and passive investment income are not counted. The practical goal for an equity-heavy tech worker is a benefit sized to total earned compensation, not just base salary, which is what most employer group coverage misses.

tech-startup-equity.title: Disability Insurance for Startup & Pre-IPO Tech Employees
tech-startup-equity.description: Startups often offer little or no group long-term disability, and your equity is illiquid until it produces income. How carriers underwrite a startup employee's salary today, why options and pre-IPO shares are not counted, and how to use a future increase option to grow the benefit after a liquidity event.
tech-startup-equity.tldr: Most startups offer little or no group long-term disability, so an early-stage employee is often almost entirely uninsured for income protection by default. Carriers underwrite earned income that has already been received and documented, which generally means your cash salary today. Stock options and pre-IPO shares are not counted until they produce W-2 income. The practical move is to buy an individual policy early while you are young, healthy, and cheap to insure, then use a future increase option to raise the benefit later as your income grows or your equity becomes liquid, with no new medical underwriting.

any-occupation-vs-own-occupation.title: Any-Occupation vs. Own-Occupation Disability Insurance
any-occupation-vs-own-occupation.description: Own-occupation pays if you cannot do your own job, even if you can work elsewhere. Any-occupation pays only if you cannot work at all. Why the distinction decides claims for high-income professionals, and where each definition shows up.
any-occupation-vs-own-occupation.tldr: Own-occupation covers you if you cannot perform your specific occupation, even if you work and earn in another field. Any-occupation covers you only if you cannot work in any occupation you're reasonably suited for. The gap matters most for professionals with transferable skills, and group plans almost always land on the weaker side of it.

benefit-period.title: Benefit Period Explained: How Long Disability Insurance Pays
benefit-period.description: The benefit period sets how long a disability policy pays. 87% of the policies in our placed book run to age 65 (2026 audit). Learn the trade-offs and the mental/nervous cap.
benefit-period.tldr: The benefit period is the maximum length of time a policy pays a claim. To-age-65 is the dominant choice: 87% of the policies in our placed book carry it (2026 audit), paired with a 90-day elimination period. Shorter periods cost less but leave a gap if a disability outlasts them, and a separate mental/nervous limitation caps psychiatric claims at 24 months only for a defined high-risk occupation group.

best-disability-insurance-companies.title: Best Disability Insurance Companies for 2026
best-disability-insurance-companies.description: Guardian, Principal, MassMutual, The Standard, and Ameritas ranked from our placement experience: own-occupation contracts, financial ratings, underwriting posture, and who each company actually fits.
best-disability-insurance-companies.tldr: Five companies write nearly all of the true own-occupation disability coverage placed on high-earning professionals: Guardian, Principal, MassMutual, The Standard, and Ameritas. No single one wins every case. Our ranking from placement experience puts Guardian first on contract strength and financial ratings, Principal first when underwriting gets complicated, and the other three ahead for specific buyers, from dividend-paying policies to the highest business overhead limits. The reliable answer for any one person is a side-by-side quote across all five.

best-disability-insurance-for-crnas.title: Best Disability Insurance Companies for CRNAs (2026)
best-disability-insurance-for-crnas.description: MassMutual, Guardian, Principal, Ameritas, and The Standard ranked for CRNAs from our placement experience. Four of the five can be written true own-occupation.
best-disability-insurance-for-crnas.tldr: Four of the five major carriers can write a CRNA with true own-occupation coverage; The Standard is the exception because its Own Occupation Rider is not available at the 2P class it assigns nurse anesthetists. MassMutual leads our CRNA ranking after upgrading CRNAs to its 4A class in 2024, with Guardian and Principal close behind. The right carrier still depends on your health history and priorities, and every CRNA policy at every major carrier limits mental and nervous claims to 24 months.

best-disability-insurance-for-dentists.title: Best Disability Insurance Companies for Dentists (2026)
best-disability-insurance-for-dentists.description: Guardian, MassMutual, The Standard, Principal, and Ameritas ranked for dentists from our placement experience: specialty recognition, dental classes, and BOE limits.
best-disability-insurance-for-dentists.tldr: Every one of the five major carriers can write a dentist with true own-occupation coverage, so the best company for you comes down to specialty recognition, occupation class, health history, and whether you own a practice. Our ranking from placement experience puts Guardian first for its dental specialty definition, with MassMutual, The Standard, Principal, and Ameritas each winning specific dentist scenarios, from residency discounts to the highest business overhead expense limit we place.

best-disability-insurance-for-physicians.title: Best Disability Insurance Companies for Physicians (2026)
best-disability-insurance-for-physicians.description: Guardian, Principal, MassMutual, The Standard, and Ameritas ranked for physicians, from our placement experience: contract strength, specialty recognition, and underwriting.
best-disability-insurance-for-physicians.tldr: There is no single best disability insurance company for every physician. All five major carriers can be written true own-occupation for most medical specialties, and the right fit turns on your specialty, your health history, and which contract provisions you care about most. The ranking below reflects Seaworthy's placement experience: Guardian leads on contract strength in our view, Principal on underwriting flexibility, MassMutual on specialty recognition and dividends, with The Standard and Ameritas each carrying real strengths of their own.

best-disability-insurance-for-residents.title: Best Disability Insurance for Medical Residents and Fellows (2026)
best-disability-insurance-for-residents.description: All five major carriers run dedicated resident programs: $5,000 to $8,000 a month with no income documentation, group LTD disregarded, resident discounts, and future increase rights. The full five-carrier comparison for residents and fellows.
best-disability-insurance-for-residents.tldr: Every one of the five major carriers runs a dedicated program for medical residents and fellows: coverage of roughly $5,000 to $8,000 a month with no income documentation, group LTD generally disregarded, resident discounts of 10 to 20 percent, and future increase rights that let the policy grow to attending income without new medical underwriting. The programs differ in the details that matter: The Standard and MassMutual publish the highest no-documentation limits, Guardian gives residents a 3x future increase multiple, Ameritas extends its 15 percent discount to attending physicians at teaching hospitals, and windows to apply run from roughly a year before graduation to as much as two years after. The bigger lever than any discount is timing: applying while your record is clean is what keeps exclusions off the contract for the rest of your career.

broker-vs-direct-disability-insurance.title: Should You Buy Disability Insurance Through a Broker or Directly?
broker-vs-direct-disability-insurance.description: What buying disability insurance direct from a carrier or captive agent means, what an independent broker actually does, when direct is fine, why carrier comparison matters in this product, and how broker compensation works.
broker-vs-direct-disability-insurance.tldr: Buying disability insurance directly from a carrier or its captive agent means choosing from one company's products at that company's filed rates. An independent broker quotes the same need across multiple carriers, compares the contract language behind the prices, and negotiates underwriting outcomes when a file draws an exclusion or rating. Direct can work fine when the carrier in question already fits your occupation and health profile. Comparison earns its keep because carriers class the same occupation differently, deliver own-occupation protection through different mechanisms, and underwrite the same medical history to different conclusions. Brokers are paid by the carrier through commissions built into filed rates, rather than through a fee added for the client.

carrier-specific-advantages.title: Carrier-Specific Advantages: How the Five Majors Actually Differ
carrier-specific-advantages.description: Guardian, MassMutual, Principal, Ameritas, and The Standard each have real strengths. Here is how we compare all five on contract language and fit, not price.
carrier-specific-advantages.tldr: The five major disability carriers each have a genuine, distinct strength: Guardian's contract and claims reputation, MassMutual's dividends and military and resident discounts, Principal's deep rider menu and flexible underwriting, Ameritas's high business-overhead limit, and The Standard's contract clarity and Family Care Benefit. We compare all five on contract language and fit for your occupation, not on price alone.

catastrophic-disability-rider.title: Catastrophic Disability Rider: When the Extra Layer Is Worth It
catastrophic-disability-rider.description: A catastrophic disability rider adds benefit for severe impairment (loss of 2+ ADLs). It is rare in practice and the cost-to-value math is usually unfavorable.
catastrophic-disability-rider.tldr: A catastrophic disability rider adds benefit on top of your base coverage when a disability is severe enough that you cannot perform two or more activities of daily living. The protection is real, but catastrophic disabilities are uncommon, and the cost-to-expected-value math is usually unfavorable. It is a situational add-on we recommend for specific risk profiles rather than a default.

cola-rider.title: Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) Rider: Protecting Benefits Against Inflation
cola-rider.description: A COLA rider raises your disability benefit during a long claim so inflation does not erode it. See per-carrier structures and when the rider earns its premium.
cola-rider.tldr: A COLA rider increases your monthly benefit during a long claim so inflation does not quietly erode its value. It matters most for younger buyers with long benefit periods and loses value once you are past roughly age 50. COLA has become standard practice in our placements: over 70% of the policies we placed in the last two years include one (2026 book audit), and we recommend it for most buyers under 50.

disability-insurance-claims-process.title: How a Disability Insurance Claim Actually Works
disability-insurance-claims-process.description: Total disability pays the fixed benefit your policy was issued for. The carrier verifies income at underwriting, not at claim. Here is how a claim really works.
disability-insurance-claims-process.tldr: A total-disability claim pays the fixed monthly benefit your policy was issued for. The carrier does not recalculate your pre-disability income at claim time, because income is verified at underwriting. Residual claims use your prior earnings, and passive income such as investments, dividends, and rent is excluded from the calculation entirely.

disability-insurance-cost.title: How Much Does Disability Insurance Cost? What High Earners Actually Pay
disability-insurance-cost.description: Individual disability insurance typically runs about 1-3% of annual income. Learn the factors that set the premium and why buying earlier costs less.
disability-insurance-cost.tldr: Individual disability insurance typically costs about 1 to 3 percent of annual income, but that range is wide because several factors set the price. Age and health are the largest levers, and both only move one direction over time, so applying earlier almost always costs less. Cost should follow the coverage decision, not lead it.

disability-insurance-for-locum-tenens.title: Disability Insurance for Locum Tenens and 1099 Physicians
disability-insurance-for-locum-tenens.description: How locum tenens and 1099 physicians document variable income for underwriting, secure true own-occupation coverage, and own a portable policy with no employer plan to fall back on.
disability-insurance-for-locum-tenens.tldr: Locum tenens and other 1099 physicians have no employer group plan and variable, multi-source income, which makes individual coverage both essential and a documentation exercise. Carriers underwrite earned income using a few years of tax returns and 1099s or W-2s, commonly averaging across years, and they exclude passive income. The two features that matter most are a true own-occupation definition and the portability of an individual policy, which travels with you across assignments and structures.

disability-insurance-myths-high-earners.title: Disability Insurance Myths That Cost High Earners Money
disability-insurance-myths-high-earners.description: Three myths cost high earners the most: that group coverage is enough, that a policy replaces a flat 60% of income, and that being healthy means you can wait. Here is what the data shows.
disability-insurance-myths-high-earners.tldr: The myths that cost high earners the most are that employer group coverage is enough, that a disability policy replaces a flat 60% of income, and that being healthy now means you can safely wait. Group LTD caps at $10,000 to $15,000, covers base only, and is taxable; individual benefits are sized in dollars to your income, so the move is to secure the carrier maximum rather than chase a percentage; and waiting is the riskiest myth, because exclusions and ratings tied to documented conditions show up on about 28% of the policies we place.

disability-insurance-riders-explained.title: Disability Insurance Riders Explained: What Each One Does and Whether It's Worth the Premium
disability-insurance-riders-explained.description: What each disability insurance rider does, whether it earns its premium for a high earner, and which ones our clients actually adopt. Grounded in our placed-book data.
disability-insurance-riders-explained.tldr: Riders turn a base disability policy into coverage that fits how you actually earn, but they are not equal value. Residual is the foundation and almost always earns its cost, because most claims are partial rather than total. A COLA rider is high value under about 45; a future increase option is essential early in a career; return of premium, catastrophic, and social insurance supplement riders rarely clear the bar for high earners. Our own placement practice reflects this: over 70% of our placements in the last two years include COLA (2026 book audit), and most new policies include a benefit-increase feature.

disability-insurance-tax-guide.title: Disability Insurance and Taxes: What High Earners Need to Know
disability-insurance-tax-guide.description: IRS Pub 525: employer-paid group premiums make benefits taxable; after-tax individual premiums make them tax-free. See the net-of-tax math for high earners.
disability-insurance-tax-guide.tldr: The IRS rule is simple: who pays the premium decides whether the benefit is taxed. Per Publication 525, employer-paid group premiums make the benefit taxable, while after-tax individual premiums make it tax-free. For a high earner, a taxable benefit loses roughly 30 to 40 percent to combined federal and state tax, so a $10,000 group benefit nets about $6,000 to $7,000. Structuring premiums so the benefit is tax-free is one of the highest-value decisions in a disability plan.

elimination-period.title: Elimination Period Explained: The Waiting Period Before Benefits Begin
elimination-period.description: The elimination period is the wait before benefits start. 90 days is the standard in our placed book. Compare 60, 90, and 180 days and how each affects premium.
elimination-period.tldr: The elimination period is the number of days you must be disabled before benefits begin, like a deductible measured in time. A 90-day period is the standard: 82% of the policies in our placed book carry one (2026 audit), paired with a to-age-65 benefit period. A shorter wait costs more; a longer wait costs less but means self-insuring for longer.

exclusion-riders.title: Exclusion Riders: How Common They Are and How We Get Them Removed
exclusion-riders.description: About 28% of the policies we place carry an exclusion or rating. Here is what they are, which professions see the most, and how exclusions get removed.
exclusion-riders.tldr: An exclusion rider carves a specific condition out of a disability policy in exchange for issuing coverage rather than declining it. In our placed book (2026 audit), roughly 28% of policies carry an exclusion or a rating, with mental and nervous history the single most common cause. An exclusion may be permanent, but in our experience it often is not: we negotiate for ratings and exclusions to be reconsiderable, and we have strong success getting them removed, commonly about two years after issue once a clean interval passes.

future-increase-options.title: Future Increase Option (FIO): Locking In Insurability Before It Costs You
future-increase-options.description: FIO lets you raise your disability benefit later without new medical underwriting, locking insurability before a health event or exclusion can limit you. Why it matters early.
future-increase-options.tldr: The future increase option lets you raise your disability benefit later without new medical underwriting. Its real job is locking in insurability before a health event, an exclusion, or a rating can limit you. That matters because roughly 28% of policies in our placed book come back with an exclusion or rating; once your health changes, new coverage can be limited or priced up. FIO is the name Guardian uses; each carrier offers its own version of the benefit-increase feature under its own name. The feature is most valuable early in a career, and most new policies we place include some form of it.

graded-vs-level-premium.title: Graded vs. Level Premium Disability Insurance: How to Choose
graded-vs-level-premium.description: Level premium is the standard for career buyers; graded eases early-career cash flow but costs more long-term. How to choose by career stage, with median age at issue 36.
graded-vs-level-premium.tldr: A level premium stays flat for the life of the policy and is the standard structure for career buyers who intend to hold coverage to retirement. A graded premium starts lower and rises for the first several years, easing early-career cash flow but costing more over a long hold. With a median age at issue of 36 across our book, most buyers have a long enough horizon that level is the default.

group-vs-individual.title: Group vs. Individual Disability Insurance: Why High Earners Need Both
group-vs-individual.description: Individual own-occupation coverage is indemnity: it pays regardless of other income. Group LTD coordinates, caps, and is taxable. See why high earners need both.
group-vs-individual.tldr: The core difference is structural. An individual own-occupation policy is indemnity, so it pays its stated monthly benefit regardless of any other coverage. Group LTD coordinates with other income, caps the benefit (commonly $10,000 to $15,000), covers base salary only, holds its own-occupation definition for only about 24 months, and is usually taxable when the employer pays. Those limits leave a large gap for a high earner, which individual coverage is built to close.

guaranteed-renewable-vs-noncancelable.title: Guaranteed Renewable vs. Noncancelable Disability Insurance: The Two Guarantees
guaranteed-renewable-vs-noncancelable.description: Two guarantees control a disability policy. Noncancelable locks premium and terms; guaranteed renewable locks terms but lets premiums rise. Noncancelable is the professional standard the five majors offer.
guaranteed-renewable-vs-noncancelable.tldr: Disability policies carry two renewal guarantees. Guaranteed renewable locks your benefits and terms but lets the carrier raise premiums by class. Noncancelable locks both the premium and the terms to a stated age, usually 65. Noncancelable plus guaranteed renewable is the standard structure for professionals, and all five major carriers we place write it.

guaranteed-standard-issue-disability-ins.title: How Guaranteed Standard Issue (GSI) Disability Insurance Works
guaranteed-standard-issue-disability-ins.description: Guaranteed standard issue (GSI) disability insurance gives eligible employees, most often physicians at hospital systems, an individual policy at a guaranteed amount with no medical underwriting. What GSI is, who can get it, the own-occupation question, the three catches, and how it layers with individual coverage.
guaranteed-standard-issue-disability-ins.tldr: Guaranteed standard issue (GSI) disability insurance is employer-sponsored coverage that issues an individual disability policy at a guaranteed amount with no medical underwriting; health history, prior exclusions, and ratings do not affect issue at the GSI amount. It is real individual coverage on a non-cancelable policy the participant owns and keeps if they change jobs, with true own-occupation available, though only an employer can sponsor the case and coverage above the guaranteed amount requires full underwriting. Seaworthy does not place GSI; we help evaluate how a GSI offer fits alongside individual coverage.

how-much-disability-insurance-do-i-need.title: How Much Disability Insurance Do You Need? Sizing Coverage for High Earners
how-much-disability-insurance-do-i-need.description: The benefit is income-based, not a flat 60 percent. Carriers issue a maximum dollar benefit set by your income. Secure that maximum, sized to your obligations, and grow it as income rises.
how-much-disability-insurance-do-i-need.tldr: There is no flat percentage rule. The maximum a carrier will issue is a dollar figure set by your documented income, and for high earners it can run from roughly $10,000 a month into the high teens. The most a single carrier will typically issue tops out around $20,000 a month for the highest earners, and it varies by state and specialty. The right approach is to secure the maximum issuable benefit, size it to your real obligations, structure it with a true own-occupation definition and residual coverage, and grow it with a future increase option as your income climbs.

how-to-choose-a-disability-insurance-adv.title: How to Choose a Disability Insurance Advisor
how-to-choose-a-disability-insurance-adv.description: A buyer's framework for choosing a disability insurance advisor. How to weigh specialization, independence, credentials, and track record, what the CLU, ChFC, and CFP designations actually mean, and how to verify an advisor before you trust them with your income.
how-to-choose-a-disability-insurance-adv.tldr: Weigh four things when choosing a disability insurance advisor. How much of the advisor's practice is disability insurance for your profession, whether they are independent and can compare the major carriers, whether they hold a recognized credential such as the CLU, ChFC, or CFP, and whether their experience with your situation is verifiable. Treat a credential as the floor and specialization as the differentiator. No designation is specific to disability insurance, so the letters signal broad rigor, and depth in this one product comes from focus and carrier access.

long-term-vs-short-term-disability.title: Long-Term vs. Short-Term Disability Insurance: What High Earners Need to Know
long-term-vs-short-term-disability.description: Short-term covers months; long-term covers years. For high earners, individual long-term coverage fills the gap above the group cap and stays portable.
long-term-vs-short-term-disability.tldr: Short-term disability covers a brief recovery, usually a few months. Long-term disability is the protection that matters for a serious claim, and for high earners it has to be individual. Group long-term commonly caps at $10,000 to $15,000 on base salary, is taxable when employer-paid, and runs own-occupation for roughly 24 months before an any-occupation test. An individual long-term policy is indemnity, portable, and fills the long-term gap above the group cap.

mental-nervous-limitations.title: Mental and Nervous Limitations in Disability Insurance: Who Faces the 24-Month Cap
mental-nervous-limitations.description: Full-benefit-period mental health coverage is available across all five major disability carriers for most professions. Learn who faces the 24-month cap and how to avoid it.
mental-nervous-limitations.tldr: The 24-month mental and nervous cap is not universal. For most professions, full-benefit-period mental health coverage is available across all five major carriers, by default or by election. The cap is required only for a high-risk group: anesthesiology, emergency medicine, pain management, nurse anesthetists, and general dentistry. Because mental and nervous conditions are the single most common reason a policy comes back with an exclusion in our placed book, the real lever is applying before any mental-health history is on record.

multi-life-disability-insurance.title: Multi-Life Disability Insurance for Firms and Practices
multi-life-disability-insurance.description: Multi-life lets a firm's professionals buy individual own-occupation policies together at a premium discount, through one coordinated arrangement, while each person owns a portable contract.
multi-life-disability-insurance.tldr: Multi-life is a way for a firm or practice to put its professionals on individual own-occupation policies through one coordinated arrangement, usually with a premium discount for the group. Each participant owns their own contract with their own benefit and own-occupation definition, so the coverage stays portable and individually owned. It pairs the contract quality of individual coverage with the efficiency and pricing of buying together.

northwestern-mutual-disability-proposal-.title: Reviewing a Northwestern Mutual Disability Insurance Proposal
northwestern-mutual-disability-proposal-.description: Six things to verify on a Northwestern Mutual disability insurance illustration before signing: which definition of total disability it uses, the mental health limitation and buy-up, the residual rider, the guaranteed maximum premium behind the dividend projection, the future increase option, and how it compares to the independent market.
northwestern-mutual-disability-proposal-.tldr: A Northwestern Mutual disability proposal can be a strong contract or an ordinary one, and the brand name does not tell you which. The six checks that decide it: whether the illustration uses the True Own Occupation or Medical True Own Occupation definition rather than the standard one, whether the mental and nervous limitation is capped at 24 months or bought up to the full benefit period, whether a residual rider covers partial disability, what the guaranteed maximum premium is behind the dividend-adjusted projection, whether a future increase option protects your insurability, and how the whole package prices against the five-carrier independent market on your exact profile.

northwestern-mutual-vs-guardian-disabili.title: Northwestern Mutual vs Guardian Disability Insurance
northwestern-mutual-vs-guardian-disabili.description: A provision-level comparison of Northwestern Mutual's TT series and Guardian's Provider Choice for physicians and dentists: own-occupation definitions after NWM's 2022 changes, mental health coverage, dividends vs guaranteed cost, and distribution.
northwestern-mutual-vs-guardian-disabili.tldr: Northwestern Mutual and Guardian are both top-rated carriers whose strongest own-occupation definitions are closer than the older physician-finance reviews suggest, especially since NWM's December 2022 definition expansion. The durable differences are mental health coverage (Guardian covers most occupations for the full benefit period by default; NWM commonly applies a 24-month limitation with a buy-up), pricing structure (NWM's participating policies project dividends that are not guaranteed; Guardian sells a fixed guaranteed cost), and distribution (an NWM advisor shows one carrier; Guardian is sold through independent brokers who compare it against the market). On both shelves, the strongest definition is elective, so the illustration in your hand decides more than the brand does.

own-occupation-by-carrier-comparison.title: Own-Occupation Definitions Compared Across the Top Carriers
own-occupation-by-carrier-comparison.description: How Guardian, Principal, MassMutual, Ameritas, and The Standard actually define own-occupation. Which build it into the base contract, which use a rider, where occupation class limits availability, and how residual coverage compares.
own-occupation-by-carrier-comparison.tldr: All five major individual carriers can be written as true own-occupation for most professions. Guardian and Ameritas build it into the base definition; MassMutual and Principal deliver it through their own-occupation definition or rider; The Standard through a rider whose availability depends on occupation class. None of the contracts name a specialty; the definition plus your occupation class is what governs.

own-occupation-disability-insurance.title: Own-Occupation Disability Insurance: What It Means and Why It Matters
own-occupation-disability-insurance.description: Own-occupation is the single most important provision that decides whether a disability claim pays. What true own-occupation means, how it differs from modified and any-occupation definitions, and what to verify before you buy.
own-occupation-disability-insurance.tldr: A true own-occupation policy pays if you cannot perform your own occupation, even if you choose to work in another job and keep earning. A modified definition stops paying once you work elsewhere; any-occupation pays only if you cannot work at all. What decides a claim is the definition you bought, applied to the duties of your occupation at the time disability begins. The definition is locked at application, so the time to get it right is before you ever file a claim.

presumptive-disability.title: Presumptive Disability: When Full Benefits Begin Immediately
presumptive-disability.description: Presumptive disability pays the full benefit, usually with no elimination period, for loss of sight, hearing, speech, or use of limbs. It is broadly available across the major carriers.
presumptive-disability.tldr: Presumptive disability pays the full monthly benefit, usually with no elimination period, when you suffer a defined catastrophic loss: sight, hearing, speech, or use of limbs. It presumes total disability without the normal proof of income loss or occupational testing, and it is broadly available across the major carriers, generally built into the base contract or included at no extra cost.

residual-disability-benefits.title: Residual Disability Benefits: How Partial-Loss Coverage Actually Pays
residual-disability-benefits.description: Most disability claims are partial, not total, so residual is the provision high earners use most. Over 95% of the policies in our placed book carry a residual rider (2026 audit). How it pays on a 15-20% income loss.
residual-disability-benefits.tldr: Residual disability, also called partial disability, pays a proportional benefit when a covered illness or injury reduces your income, not only when you cannot work at all. Most disabilities are partial, so this is the provision most high earners actually use, and over 95% of the policies in our placed book carry a residual rider (2026 audit). Across the five major carriers we place, the trigger is a 15% income loss (20% at The Standard), all five pay roughly a 50% minimum early in a claim, all include a recovery benefit for the return-to-work ramp, and none require a prior period of total disability. Because carrier issue limits cap the maximum benefit below a high earner's full income, residual is the part of the contract that does the most work over a career.

retirement-protection-rider.title: Retirement Protection Rider: Who It Actually Helps
retirement-protection-rider.description: A retirement protection rider keeps retirement contributions going during a disability. It is context-dependent and works best for young, long-horizon buyers.
retirement-protection-rider.tldr: A retirement protection rider replaces the retirement savings you would lose during a disability, typically by paying a separate benefit into a trust that is invested for retirement and released at your normal retirement age. Its value is context-dependent and rises with time horizon, so it favors younger buyers, which fits our book: the median age at issue is 36. For late-career buyers there is little horizon left to protect.

return-of-premium-rider.title: Return of Premium Rider: The Opportunity-Cost Problem
return-of-premium-rider.description: A return-of-premium rider can add roughly 30-50% to your base premium. For most high earners the opportunity cost makes it rarely worth it.
return-of-premium-rider.tldr: A return-of-premium rider refunds a portion of premiums if you reach a set age without a claim, but it adds roughly 30 to 50% to your base premium to do it. For most high earners the opportunity cost is the catch: the same dollars invested elsewhere typically grow to more than the refund, and the refund disappears entirely if you do claim. We rarely place it.

student-loan-rider.title: Student Loan Rider: Protecting Education Debt During a Disability
student-loan-rider.description: A student loan rider pays your education debt during a disability, separate from your base benefit. Most useful for residents and early-career professionals.
student-loan-rider.tldr: A student loan rider pays a benefit toward your education debt during a disability, on top of your base benefit, so a long claim does not put your loans into default. It matters most for residents and early-career professionals carrying large balances, and it is a strong reason to apply early. MassMutual runs resident discount programs commonly reaching 20% for medical and 10% for dental residents, which makes locking in coverage in training especially efficient.

when-to-buy-disability-insurance.title: When to Buy Disability Insurance: Why Earlier Almost Always Wins
when-to-buy-disability-insurance.description: The median age at issue in our book is 36, and about 28% of policies get an exclusion or rating. Apply before health events to protect price and coverage.
when-to-buy-disability-insurance.tldr: The best time to buy disability insurance is while you are young and healthy, because age and health are the two largest levers on both price and coverage and both only move one direction over time. In our placed book the median age at issue is 36, and about 28 percent of policies end up with an exclusion or a rating. Applying before a health event is the most reliable way to keep coverage broad and the price low.

ameritas.title: Ameritas Disability Insurance Review: DInamic Cornerstone
ameritas.description: A provision-level review of Ameritas DInamic Cornerstone (form 4601NC): true own-occupation in the base definition, a residual rider that pays full loss for the first three months, a mental-health cap that excludes neurocognitive disease, the highest BOE limit of the majors, and the conservative underwriting that defines the carrier.
ameritas.tldr: Ameritas DInamic Cornerstone (form 4601NC) puts true own-occupation in the base definition, no rider required, and pairs it with strong early-claim residual mechanics (full loss paid for the first three months) and a mental-health limitation that notably excludes neurocognitive disease. Ameritas carries the highest business-overhead-expense limit of the majors ($100,000 a month). The trade-off is underwriting: in our experience it sits toward the conservative end of the five, so it rewards clean, well-documented files.

guardian.title: Guardian Disability Insurance Review: Provider Choice Contract
guardian.description: A provision-level review of Guardian's Provider Choice (issued by Berkshire Life, form 18ID): true own-occupation definition options, the strongest mental-health coverage of the majors, residual at a 15% income-loss threshold, COLA variants, catastrophic riders, and who it fits.
guardian.tldr: Guardian's Provider Choice, issued by Berkshire Life (form 18ID), is, in our view, the strongest individual disability contract for high earners. It offers a true own-occupation definition for the full benefit period (with specialty and MD/DO-enhanced variants), and for most occupations places no time cap on mental and nervous claims, the strongest position of the five carriers we place (the higher-risk specialties, including anesthesiology, ER, pain management, and nurse anesthetists, are required to take the 24-month limitation, as they are everywhere). Its partial-disability rider triggers at a 15% income loss with no time-or-duties requirement. The trade-offs are higher premiums and more stringent underwriting: Guardian generally sits at the higher end on price and is, in our experience, the strictest of the five to move on a borderline file.

massmutual.title: MassMutual Disability Insurance Review: Radius Choice
massmutual.description: A provision-level review of MassMutual Radius Choice (form ICC15-XLIS-RC): true own-occupation via the Own Occupation Rider with billing-code specialty recognition, a 3% compound no-cap COLA, the mental-health endorsement that removes the 24-month cap, dividend potential, and the only major that writes active-duty military.
massmutual.tldr: MassMutual Radius Choice (form ICC15-XLIS-RC) is a participating, dividend-eligible contract from a mutual company. It delivers true own-occupation through its Own Occupation Rider, with specialty recognition tied to CPT/ADA billing codes, and carries a 3% compound COLA with no cap. It is one of the few carriers that can extend mental-health coverage past the 24-month cap (by endorsement, outside California), and, to our knowledge, the only major that will write a policy for active-duty military, with military, government, and resident discounts.

northwestern-mutual.title: Northwestern Mutual Disability Insurance Review
northwestern-mutual.description: A provision-level review of Northwestern Mutual's individual disability insurance (TT series) from an independent brokerage that does not sell it: the 2022 definition changes, Medical True Own Occupation, dividends, the 24-month mental health limitation, and what to verify on a proposal.
northwestern-mutual.tldr: Northwestern Mutual is the largest individual disability income insurer in the country by direct premiums earned (per S&P Capital IQ Pro data cited by the company), with top-tier financial ratings and participating policies that pay dividends. Since December 2022 it has offered medical professionals a choice of true own-occupation definitions, which makes the older blanket criticism of its contracts partially outdated. Seaworthy does not sell Northwestern Mutual, because it distributes only through its own advisors; we review it because so many of our clients are holding an NWM proposal when they call, and the question that decides everything is which definition of total disability that specific proposal uses.

principal.title: Principal Disability Insurance Review: Income Protector
principal.description: A provision-level review of Principal's Income Protector (form ICC22-800): true own-occupation as placed, two no-cost benefit-growth riders, a no-cost presumptive rider with no elimination period, a generous residual benefit, and one of the deepest rider menus of the major carriers. Plus the underwriting flexibility we rely on.
principal.tldr: Principal Income Protector (form ICC22-800) is a top-tier individual disability contract on its own merits: true own-occupation as we place it, two no-cost growth riders (3% automatic annual increase plus a no-medical benefit-increase rider), a no-cost presumptive benefit with no elimination period, a residual rider that pays a 50% floor for the first year and treats a 75% loss as total, and a deep menu including catastrophic, lump-sum cancer/stroke, and business-protection riders. As a bonus, its underwriting is, in our experience, the most flexible of the five, which is what saves a complicated case.

the-standard.title: The Standard Disability Insurance Review: Platinum Advantage
the-standard.description: A provision-level review of The Standard's Platinum Advantage: a regular-occupation base with true own-occupation via a class-gated rider (3A/3P/3D and higher), three residual tiers at a 20% threshold, a 3%/6% COLA choice, a Family Care Benefit, and a strong student-loan rider. Where it fits and where occupation class decides.
the-standard.tldr: The Standard's Platinum Advantage is a clear, well-built contract whose true own-occupation comes through an Own Occupation Rider available only to occupation classes 3A/3P/3D and higher. The base definition is a regular-occupation definition. It offers three residual tiers (20% income-loss threshold), a choice of 3% or 6% COLA, an unusual Family Care Benefit, and a student-loan rider up to $2,500 a month. Occupation class, more than the carrier, decides what you can get.

ada-disability-plan.title: The ADA Disability Plan for Dentists: What It Covers and Where It Falls Short
ada-disability-plan.description: The ADA-sponsored disability plan from Protective: premiums that step up every five years and can be changed for the group annually, residual benefits that require a prior total disability, the $15,000 cap, membership-tied coverage, and where an individual policy is the stronger core.
ada-disability-plan.tldr: The ADA Disability Income Protection Plan, underwritten by Protective, is a group certificate with structural limits a high-earning dentist outgrows: premiums step up every five years on attained age and the group's rates can change as often as once every 12 months, the base residual benefit pays only after a prior total disability, and the $15,000 ceiling cannot be raised past the plan maximum. Coverage also ends if you leave the ADA, stop working full time, retire, or the Association terminates the group policy. An individual policy closes each of those gaps with a level non-cancelable premium, residual that pays on income loss alone, benefit capacity sized to income, and a contract you own regardless of memberships.

ama-group-disability.title: The AMA-Sponsored Disability Plan for Physicians: What It Covers and Where It Falls Short
ama-group-disability.description: The AMA-sponsored group disability plan from New York Life: age-banded premiums, a one-time three-year benefit increase window, the 24-month mental and nervous cap, conditional renewability, and where an individual policy is the stronger core.
ama-group-disability.tldr: The AMA-sponsored disability plan, underwritten by New York Life, is group coverage with structural limits a high-earning physician outgrows. Premiums increase at every age bracket and rates can be raised class-wide for the whole group. Renewal requires that you remain a physician actively at work, that the group policy stays in force, and that the AMA keeps sponsoring it; retire early and the coverage ends. The benefit increase option is a one-time election within three years of issue and before age 40, mental and nervous claims cap at 24 months, residual benefits require a prior total disability, and combined coverage cannot exceed 66 2/3% of income or $30,000 a month. An individual policy closes each of those gaps: a level non-cancelable premium, an increase option open typically to age 55, full-period mental and nervous coverage for most specialties, residual that pays on income loss alone, and renewal terms fixed at issue.

riders.name: Residual (Partial) Disability
riders.summary: Pays a proportional benefit when a covered disability reduces income by roughly 15-20% or more. Most disabilities are partial, not total; without this rider a policy only pays when you cannot work at all.

riders.name: Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA)
riders.summary: Increases the monthly benefit during long claims to keep pace with inflation. Compound 3% is the standard structure. Value drops materially past age 50 because the remaining benefit horizon shortens.

riders.name: Future Increase Option (FIO)
riders.summary: Locks in insurability. Lets the insured buy more coverage as income rises without new medical underwriting. Typically available until age 55 or a set number of years.

riders.name: Own-Occupation Enhancement
riders.audience: anyone with a modified-own-occ base policy
riders.summary: Extends the true own-occupation definition if the base contract is modified own-occ. Not needed when the base policy is already true own-occ to age 65.

riders.name: Retirement Protection
riders.audience: high earners with significant retirement-savings goals
riders.summary: Continues retirement-fund contributions during a disability. Valuable with a long career horizon and large retirement-savings targets; less valuable for late-career buyers.

riders.name: Return of Premium
riders.summary: Adds roughly 30-50% to the base premium. The opportunity cost of that extra premium invested elsewhere almost always exceeds the returned amount.

riders.name: Catastrophic Disability
riders.summary: Adds benefit for severe disabilities (loss of two or more activities of daily living). Coverage is meaningful but catastrophic disabilities are rare; cost-to-expected-value is typically unfavorable.

riders.name: Social Insurance Supplement
riders.summary: Pays if a Social Security disability claim is denied. Most high earners will not qualify for SSDI under the any-occupation standard, so the trigger rarely fires usefully.
